Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". file.content:
name: Load Tests

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      environment:
        description: 'Target environment'
        required: true
        default: 'local'
        type: choice
        options:
          - local
          - staging
      client_count:
        description: 'Number of concurrent clients'
        required: false
        default: '5'
      scenario:
        description: 'Test scenario to run'
        required: true
        default: 'mixed-workload'
        type: choice
        options:
          - upload-throughput
          - ipns-publish-storm
          - mixed-workload
          - sustained-load
          - spike-test
          - byo-upload-throughput
          - byo-mixed-workload
          - byo-capacity-ceiling
      load_test_byo_endpoint:
        description: 'BYO provider endpoint (byo-* scenarios only)'
        required: false
        default: 'https://api.pinata.cloud'
      load_test_byo_protocol:
        description: 'BYO provider protocol'
        required: false
        default: 'pinata'
        type: choice
        options:
          - pinata
          - psa
          - kubo
      load_test_byo_provider_name:
        description: 'BYO provider label for reports'
        required: false
        default: 'pinata'

concurrency:
  group: load-test-${{ inputs.environment }}
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions: {}

jobs:
  load-test:
    name: 'Load Test: ${{ inputs.scenario }} (${{ inputs.client_count }} clients)'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: ${{ inputs.environment == 'staging' && 'staging' || '' }}
    timeout-minutes: 60
    permissions:
      contents: read

    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16-alpine
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: postgres
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
          POSTGRES_DB: cipherbox_test
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready
          --health-interval 10s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 5

      ipfs:
        image: ipfs/kubo:v0.40.0
        ports:
          - 5001:5001
          - 8080:8080
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "ipfs id"
          --health-interval 10s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 10
          --health-start-period 30s

      redis:
        image: redis:7-alpine
        ports:
          - 6379:6379
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "redis-cli ping"
          --health-interval 10s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 5

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0

      - name: Setup pnpm
        uses: pnpm/action-setup@0ebf47130e4866e96fce0953f49152a61190b271 # v6.0.9

      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@48b55a011bda9f5d6aeb4c2d9c7362e8dae4041e # v6.4.0
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: 'pnpm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Install mock-ipns-routing dependencies
        run: |
          cd tools/mock-ipns-routing
          npm install
          npm run build

      - name: Build packages
        run: |
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/crypto build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/core build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/api-client build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/sdk-core build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/sdk build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/api build

      - name: Create API .env
        if: inputs.environment == 'local'
        run: |
          echo "NODE_ENV=test" > apps/api/.env
          echo "DB_HOST=localhost" >> apps/api/.env
          echo "DB_PORT=5432" >> apps/api/.env
          echo "DB_USERNAME=postgres" >> apps/api/.env
          echo "DB_PASSWORD=REDACTED >> apps/api/.env
          echo "DB_DATABASE=cipherbox_test" >> apps/api/.env
          echo "JWT_SECRET=e2e-test-jwt-secret-key-for-ci" >> apps/api/.env
          echo "CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5173" >> apps/api/.env
          echo "IPFS_PROVIDER=local" >> apps/api/.env
          echo "IPFS_LOCAL_API_URL=http://localhost:5001" >> apps/api/.env
          echo "IPFS_LOCAL_GATEWAY_URL=http://localhost:8080" >> apps/api/.env
          echo "DELEGATED_ROUTING_URL=http://localhost:3001" >> apps/api/.env
          echo "REDIS_HOST=localhost" >> apps/api/.env
          echo "REDIS_PORT=6379" >> apps/api/.env
          echo "TEST_LOGIN_SECRET=e2e-test-secret-ci-only" >> apps/api/.env
          echo "IDENTITY_JWT_PRIVATE_KEY=${{ secrets.IDENTITY_JWT_PRIVATE_KEY }}" >> apps/api/.env
          echo "REDACTED" >> apps/api/.env

      - name: Start mock IPNS routing
        if: inputs.environment == 'local'
        run: |
          cd tools/mock-ipns-routing
          node dist/server.js &
          sleep 2

      - name: Start API server
        if: inputs.environment == 'local'
        run: |
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/api start:prod &
          for i in $(seq 1 30); do
            if curl -fsS http://localhost:3000/health > /dev/null 2>&1; then
              echo "API is ready"
              break
            fi
            sleep 1
          done
          if ! curl -fsS http://localhost:3000/health > /dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "API failed to start within 30s"
            exit 1
          fi
        env:
          NODE_ENV: test
          DB_HOST: localhost
          DB_PORT: 5432
          DB_USERNAME: postgres
          DB_PASSWORD: postgres
          DB_DATABASE: cipherbox_test
          JWT_SECRET: e2e-test-jwt-secret-key-for-ci
          CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS: http://localhost:5173
          IPFS_PROVIDER: local
          IPFS_LOCAL_API_URL: http://localhost:5001
          IPFS_LOCAL_GATEWAY_URL: http://localhost:8080
          DELEGATED_ROUTING_URL: http://localhost:3001
          REDIS_HOST: localhost
          REDIS_PORT: 6379
          TEST_LOGIN_SECRET: e2e-test-secret-ci-only

      - name: Set environment variables
        run: |
          if [ "${{ inputs.environment }}" = "staging" ]; then
            echo "LOAD_TEST_API_URL=${{ vars.STAGING_API_URL }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV
            echo "LOAD_TEST_SECRET=${{ secrets.STAGING_TEST_LOGIN_SECRET }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV
            echo "THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET=${{ secrets.STAGING_THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV
          else
            echo "LOAD_TEST_API_URL=http://localhost:3000" >> $GITHUB_ENV
            echo "LOAD_TEST_SECRET=e2e-test-secret-ci-only" >> $GITHUB_ENV
            echo "REDACTED" >> $GITHUB_ENV
          fi
          # BYO-IPFS provider config — only exported for byo-* scenarios
          if [[ "${{ inputs.scenario }}" == byo-* ]]; then
            if [ -z "${{ secrets.LOAD_TEST_BYO_AUTH_TOKEN }}" ]; then
              echo "::error::LOAD_TEST_BYO_AUTH_TOKEN secret is not set. Required for byo-* scenarios."
              exit 1
            fi
            echo "BYO_IPFS_ENDPOINT=${{ inputs.load_test_byo_endpoint }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV
            echo "BYO_IPFS_AUTH_TOKEN=${{ secrets.LOAD_TEST_BYO_AUTH_TOKEN }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV
            echo "BYO_IPFS_PROTOCOL=${{ inputs.load_test_byo_protocol }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV
            echo "BYO_IPFS_PROVIDER_NAME=${{ inputs.load_test_byo_provider_name }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV
          fi
          CLIENT_COUNT="${{ inputs.client_count }}"
          if ! [[ "$CLIENT_COUNT" =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]]; then
            echo "Invalid client_count: '$CLIENT_COUNT' (must be a positive integer)" >&2
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "LOAD_TEST_CLIENTS=$CLIENT_COUNT" >> $GITHUB_ENV

      - name: Run load test
        working-directory: tests/load
        run: |
          pnpm exec vitest run --no-coverage "${{ inputs.scenario }}"

      - name: Upload metrics report
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@043fb46d1a93c77aae656e7c1c64a875d1fc6a0a # v7.0.1
        with:
          name: load-test-metrics-${{ inputs.scenario }}-${{ inputs.client_count }}clients
          path: tests/load/metrics-*.json
          retention-days: 30
          if-no-files-found: ignore

input.command: grep -rilE "load.?test|k6|artillery|locust" . 2>/dev/null | grep -vE "node_modules|/dist/|/target/|pnpm-lock|\.git/" | sort | head -80
input.description: Find load-test files repo-wide

# Staging Load Tests: Running Multiple Tests Simultaneously Causes 429s

## Date: 2026-03-29

## Context

Running SDK load tests (`tests/load/`) against staging with 200 concurrent clients.
Initial runs hit 429 ThrottlerException, but investigation revealed the bypass mechanism works correctly.

## Root Cause

**Two load tests were launched simultaneously against the same staging instance** (sustained-load with 200 clients + BYO capacity ceiling with 50 clients). The combined load saturated the staging API. The throttle bypass header was being sent and accepted, but the server couldn't handle 250+ concurrent account creation flows.

## How We Confirmed

1. curl with bypass header: 20 concurrent -> all 200 OK
2. Node.js fetch with bypass header: 50 concurrent -> all 200 OK
3. vitest with `createClientPool(20)`: 20/20 in 4.7s
4. vitest with `createClientPool(50)`: 50/50 in 10.0s
5. Both tests together: 429s after ~10 accounts (server saturated)

The bypass header skips rate limiter **guards**, but doesn't make the server infinitely scalable. The staging VPS has finite resources.

## Rules

- **Never run multiple load test scenarios concurrently against staging** -- run them sequentially
- The `tests/load/.env` must be sourced before running: `set -a && source .env && set +a`
- vitest does NOT auto-load `.env` files -- env must be sourced in the shell

## Throttle Config Reference

| Setting       | CI (NODE_ENV=test) | Staging (NODE_ENV=staging) |
| ------------- | ------------------ | -------------------------- |
| Short limit   | 200/sec            | 10/sec                     |
| Medium limit  | 2000/min           | 100/min                    |
| Bypass header | Works (unneeded)   | Works (required)           |

## Key Files

- `apps/api/src/common/guards/throttler-bypass.guard.ts` -- bypass logic
- `apps/api/src/app.module.ts` -- throttle limit config (lines 59-74)
- `tests/sdk-e2e/src/fixtures/test-harness.ts` -- account creation with bypass header
- `tests/load/src/harness/client-pool.ts` -- pool creation (batches of 5)
- `tests/load/.env` -- staging load test configuration (not auto-loaded by vitest)

# @cipherbox/load-tests

Load tests for the CipherBox API and SDK. Measures upload throughput, IPNS publish
concurrency, mixed workloads, sustained traffic, spike behaviour, and BYO-IPFS provider
capacity — all against a live API target.

Part of the [CipherBox monorepo](../../README.md).

## Tooling

[Vitest](https://vitest.dev/) runs the scenarios sequentially (no parallelism). Each test
has a 10-minute timeout. Results are written to `metrics-*.json` files in this directory.

## Scenarios

| Scenario                | File                                          |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `upload-throughput`     | `src/scenarios/upload-throughput.test.ts`     |
| `ipns-publish-storm`    | `src/scenarios/ipns-publish-storm.test.ts`    |
| `mixed-workload`        | `src/scenarios/mixed-workload.test.ts`        |
| `sustained-load`        | `src/scenarios/sustained-load.test.ts`        |
| `spike-test`            | `src/scenarios/spike-test.test.ts`            |
| `byo-upload-throughput` | `src/scenarios/byo-upload-throughput.test.ts` |
| `byo-mixed-workload`    | `src/scenarios/byo-mixed-workload.test.ts`    |
| `byo-capacity-ceiling`  | `src/scenarios/byo-capacity-ceiling.test.ts`  |

## Running Locally

Set the required environment variables, then run a single scenario by name:

```bash
LOAD_TEST_API_URL=http://localhost:3000 \
LOAD_TEST_SECRET=<test-login-secret> \
THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET=<throttle-bypass-secret> \
LOAD_TEST_CLIENTS=5 \
pnpm exec vitest run --no-coverage mixed-workload
```

For BYO-IPFS scenarios, also set:

```bash
BYO_IPFS_ENDPOINT=https://api.pinata.cloud
BYO_IPFS_AUTH_TOKEN=<token>
BYO_IPFS_PROTOCOL=pinata   # pinata | psa | kubo
BYO_IPFS_PROVIDER_NAME=pinata
```

## Environment Variables

| Variable                 | Required         | Description                                          |
| ------------------------ | ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `LOAD_TEST_API_URL`      | Yes              | Base URL of the API under test                       |
| `LOAD_TEST_SECRET`       | Yes              | `TEST_LOGIN_SECRET` value used to mint test sessions |
| `THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET` | Yes              | Secret to bypass API rate limiting during load runs  |
| `LOAD_TEST_CLIENTS`      | No (default `5`) | Number of concurrent virtual clients                 |
| `BYO_IPFS_ENDPOINT`      | byo-\* only      | BYO IPFS provider base URL                           |
| `BYO_IPFS_AUTH_TOKEN`    | byo-\* only      | Auth token for the BYO provider                      |
| `BYO_IPFS_PROTOCOL`      | byo-\* only      | Provider protocol: `pinata`, `psa`, or `kubo`        |
| `BYO_IPFS_PROVIDER_NAME` | byo-\* only      | Label used in metrics output                         |

## CI

The `load-test.yml` workflow (`manual dispatch only`) runs any scenario against `local` or
`staging`. For `local` it spins up Postgres, Kubo IPFS, and Redis service containers and
starts the API before executing. Metrics JSON is uploaded as a workflow artifact
(retained 30 days).

## Related Docs

- [Testing strategy](../TESTING_STRATEGY.md)
- [Full testing reference](../../docs/TESTING.md)

16	## Methodology
17	
18	Baselines are captured using `scripts/baseline-benchmark.sh` which:
19	
20	1. Discovers the user's root IPNS name via `GET /vault`
21	2. Runs 3 warmup iterations (discarded) followed by 20 measured iterations
22	3. Measures client-side round-trip time via `curl -w "%{time_total}"`
23	4. Computes p50/p95/p99 from sorted timing values
24	5. IPNS Publish is excluded (requires signed record) -- captured from Prometheus
25	
26	Server-side histograms (`cipherbox_ipfs_ipns_duration_seconds`) provide internal timing without network overhead. Client-side timings from this script include network latency and are useful for end-to-end comparison.

29	
30	| Operation           | p50    | p95    | p99    | Notes                                   |
31	| ------------------- | ------ | ------ | ------ | --------------------------------------- |

# Performance Baselines - Phase 18

## Capture Information

| Field            | Value                                                           |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Capture Date** | 2026-03-07T16:55:31Z (updated 2026-03-08)                       |
| **Environment**  | Staging (api-staging.cipherbox.cc)                              |
| **Kubo Version** | v0.34.0                                                         |
| **API Image**    | v0.24.2-staging-rc-1                                            |
| **VPS**          | Hostinger 76.13.151.200, 4 vCPU, 8GB RAM                        |
| **Script**       | `scripts/baseline-benchmark.sh` + `tests/e2e/load-test.spec.ts` |
| **Iterations**   | 20 measured + 3 warmup per operation (benchmark script)         |
| **File Size**    | 10KB random data (upload/download) for benchmark script         |

## Methodology

Baselines are captured using `scripts/baseline-benchmark.sh` which:

1. Discovers the user's root IPNS name via `GET /vault`
2. Runs 3 warmup iterations (discarded) followed by 20 measured iterations
3. Measures client-side round-trip time via `curl -w "%{time_total}"`
4. Computes p50/p95/p99 from sorted timing values
5. IPNS Publish is excluded (requires signed record) -- captured from Prometheus

Server-side histograms (`cipherbox_ipfs_ipns_duration_seconds`) provide internal timing without network overhead. Client-side timings from this script include network latency and are useful for end-to-end comparison.

## Client-Side Timings (curl round-trip)

| Operation           | p50    | p95    | p99    | Notes                                   |
| ------------------- | ------ | ------ | ------ | --------------------------------------- |
| IPNS Resolve        | 0.147s | 0.224s | 0.278s | `GET /ipns/resolve?ipnsName=<name>`     |
| IPNS Publish        | --     | --     | --     | See Prometheus (requires signed record) |
| IPFS Pin (upload)   | 0.138s | 0.218s | 0.227s | `POST /ipfs/upload` with 10KB file      |
| IPFS Cat (download) | 0.133s | 0.215s | 0.219s | `GET /ipfs/<cid>` for 10KB file         |

## Server-Side Histograms (Prometheus)

Captured from the API's `/metrics` endpoint via SSH on 2026-03-08. Includes cumulative data from the baseline-benchmark script run (single-client, ~38 ops) plus the 5-client load test (~377 ops across 5 concurrent users).

### `cipherbox_ipfs_ipns_duration_seconds` — per-operation breakdown

Percentiles computed from Prometheus histogram buckets (linear interpolation within bucket boundaries).

| Operation        | Source  | Count | p50    | p95    | p99    | Mean   | Notes                                         |
| ---------------- | ------- | ----- | ------ | ------ | ------ | ------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| **publish**      | --      | 1367  | 180 ms | 519 ms | 904 ms | 196 ms | Kubo IPNS publish — dominant bottleneck       |
| **resolve**      | network | 529   | 135 ms | 284 ms | 488 ms | 126 ms | Kubo DHT lookup (cache miss)                  |
| **resolve**      | db      | 84    | 35 ms  | 93 ms  | 187 ms | 36 ms  | DB cache hit (success path)                   |
| **resolve** (fb) | db      | 239   | 23 ms  | 84 ms  | 230 ms | 32 ms  | DB cache fallback (Kubo resolve failed)       |
| **resolve**      | network | 42    | 231 ms | 650 ms | 930 ms | 251 ms | Network errors (Kubo resolve timeout/failure) |
| **pin**          | --      | 1923  | 8 ms   | 18 ms  | 31 ms  | 8 ms   | Kubo `pin add` — very fast for small files    |
| **cat**          | --      | 704   | 2 ms   | 5 ms   | 9 ms   | 2 ms   | Kubo `cat` — sub-5ms for cached content       |

Note: Resolve has 4 series because the API tries Kubo first (source=network), then falls back to DB cache (source=db). The `result` label distinguishes success/error at the Kubo level.

### Other histograms

| `cipherbox_republish_batch_duration_seconds` | No data | Mock TEE provider doesn't report durations |
| `cipherbox_http_request_duration_seconds`    | Below   | Per-route breakdown in HTTP table          |

## HTTP API Performance (from Prometheus)

Response times by route — computed from `cipherbox_http_request_duration_seconds` histogram (routes with ≥10 requests):

## Load Test Details

### Run 1: Manual stress test (single client)

To populate initial IPNS publish histogram data, a manual stress test was performed via Playwright against the staging web app:

| Operation     | Count      | Details                                                   |
| ------------- | ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Folder create | 8          | stress-01 through -05, nested-subfolder, rapid-fire-01–03 |
| File upload   | 13         | 10 small (7–48 KB) + 3 large (1 MB, 5 MB, 10 MB)          |
| Rename        | 4          | 2 files, 1 folder, 1 large file                           |
| Move          | 3          | Files into stress-02, stress-03, renamed-folder-01        |
| Delete        | 10         | 5 files + 5 folders (some with contents)                  |
| **Total**     | **~38–43** | Each mutates metadata → IPNS publish                      |

Concurrently, `baseline-benchmark.sh` ran 20 iterations of resolve/pin/cat (+ warmups).

### Run 2: Automated load test (5 concurrent clients)

`tests/e2e/load-test.spec.ts` — 5 clients with unique wallets, launched simultaneously (no staggering), each running ~70 file operations.

| Metric              | Value                                       |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| **Clients**         | 5 (all started at the same time)            |
| **Total ops**       | 395 attempted, 377 succeeded (95.4%)        |
| **Failed ops**      | 18 (all timeouts — 30s per-op limit)        |
| **Total time**      | 317s (5.3 minutes)                          |
| **Throughput**      | 1.25 ops/sec (aggregate across all clients) |
| **IPNS publishes**  | ~377 (one per successful mutation)          |
| **Account cleanup** | 5/5 accounts deleted                        |

Per-client breakdown:

| Client | Succeeded | Failed | Notes                                         |
| ------ | --------- | ------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| C1     | 79        | 0      | Finished first — got head start before others |
| C2     | 72        | 7      | Warm-up timeout + move dialog timeouts        |
| C3     | 78        | 1      | Single upload timeout in images folder        |
| C4     | 73        | 6      | Warm-up timeout + folder creation timeout     |
| C5     | 75        | 4      | Warm-up timeout + batch delete timeout        |

Failure pattern: C2–C5 all timed out on their warm-up folder operation (30s) while C1 raced ahead. Subsequent failures clustered around move dialog waits and folder navigation — consistent with server-side IPNS publish latency increasing under concurrent load. The 5-client workload drove ~1,300 IPNS publishes through Kubo simultaneously.

## Notes

- Client-side timings captured 2026-03-07 via `baseline-benchmark.sh` (5 runs × 20 iterations per operation = 100 data points per operation, 300 total across resolve/pin/cat)
- Server-side histogram values captured 2026-03-08 via SSH to staging VPS (`curl http://localhost:3000/metrics`) — cumulative across benchmark script + 5-client load test
- 5-client load test run 2026-03-08 via `tests/e2e/load-test.spec.ts` — 5 concurrent Playwright browsers, ~70 ops each, all launched simultaneously
- IPNS Publish is the dominant bottleneck at ~519ms p95 server-side (904ms p99) — essentially all time in Kubo, negligible HTTP overhead
- Under 5-client concurrency, publish-batch p95 reaches 793ms (vs 477ms for single publish) — batching multiple IPNS names increases latency
- IPNS Resolve network errors (n=42) have high latency (p50=231ms, p95=650ms) — these are Kubo timeouts that trigger DB cache fallback
- DB cache fallback is fast (p50=23ms) and handles 74% of resolve calls (239/323 db-path resolves were error-fallback)
- Pin and Cat remain extremely fast under load (p50=8ms and 2ms) — client-side timings (~130ms) are dominated by network latency
- Kubo v0.34.0 does not expose libp2p metrics — Kubo Health section is N/A
- TEE Republish Batch Duration shows "No data" — mock TEE provider doesn't report real durations
- These baselines will be compared against post-Phase 19 and Phase 22 measurements
- The benchmark script is deterministic: same iterations, same file size, same warmup count
- The load test script (`tests/e2e/load-test.spec.ts`) is parameterized: `LOAD_TEST_CLIENTS` env var (default: 5)

## Comparison Target

Phase 22 (after IPFS infrastructure changes) will re-run this benchmark and document:

- Performance regression threshold: >20% p95 increase requires investigation
- Performance improvement targets vary by operation (see Phase 22 plan)

118	Before the three-point comparison, a concurrency probe established the local infrastructure's concurrency ceiling using the sequential SDK + flatfs configuration:

120	| Clients | uploadFile p50 | p95      | p99      | throughput ops/s | errors         |
121	| ------- | -------------- | -------- | -------- | ---------------- | -------------- |
122	| 1       | 131ms          | 287ms    | 497ms    | 6.36             | 0              |
123	| 5       | 1,016ms        | 1,871ms  | 2,148ms  | 4.97             | 0              |
124	| 10      | 2,499ms        | 3,768ms  | 4,496ms  | 3.95             | 0              |
125	| 20      | 5,897ms        | 8,806ms  | 9,741ms  | 3.43             | 0              |
126	| 50      | 14,789ms       | 19,315ms | 21,861ms | 3.36             | 0              |
127	| 75      | 30,804ms       | 53,603ms | 59,892ms | 2.44             | 10             |
128	| 100     | --             | --       | --       | --               | many (timeout) |
129	
130	**Chosen N: 50 clients** -- the highest client count with zero errors and no timeout failures. At 75 clients, 10 errors appeared; at 100 clients, widespread timeouts occurred. The 50-client count also satisfies SC3's requirement to measure throughput at scale.
131	
132	### Three-Point Results Table (50 clients x 20 files = 1,000 uploads)
133	
134	| Metric           | Run 1 (No Opts) | Run 2 (SDK Concurrent) | Run 3 (SDK + Pebbleds) | SDK Delta (R2 vs R1) | Pebbleds Delta (R3 vs R2) | Total Delta (R3 vs R1) |
135	| ---------------- | --------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------- |
136	| uploadFile p50   | 14,664ms        | 14,664ms               | 13,860ms               | 0.0%                 | -5.5%                     | **-5.5%**              |
137	| uploadFile p95   | 18,734ms        | 44,704ms               | 16,302ms               | +138.5%              | -63.5%                    | **-13.0%**             |
138	| uploadFile p99   | 20,519ms        | 50,301ms               | 17,467ms               | +145.1%              | -65.3%                    | **-14.9%**             |
139	| uploadFile avg   | 14,791ms        | 20,061ms               | 13,984ms               | +35.6%               | -30.3%                    | **-5.5%**              |
140	| uploadFile min   | 5,463ms         | 7,194ms                | 5,453ms                | +31.7%               | -24.2%                    | -0.2%                  |
141	| uploadFile max   | 22,379ms        | 53,422ms               | 19,466ms               | +138.7%              | -63.6%                    | -13.0%                 |
142	| throughput ops/s | 3.45            | 2.54                   | 3.69                   | -26.4%               | +45.3%                    | **+7.0%**              |
143	| total duration   | 289.8s          | 394.0s                 | 271.1s                 | +35.9%               | -31.2%                    | -6.5%                  |
144	| data transferred | 250.2 MB        | 246.3 MB               | 244.7 MB               | --                   | --                        | --                     |
145	| errors           | 0               | 0                      | 0                      | --                   | --                        | --                     |
146	| datastore        | flatfs          | flatfs                 | pebbleds               | --                   | --                        | --                     |
147	| SDK mode         | sequential      | concurrent             | concurrent             | --                   | --                        | --                     |
148	
149	### Optimization Attribution
150	
151	**SDK concurrent pins alone (Run 2 vs Run 1): DEGRADED performance at 50 clients.**
152	
153	The concurrent SDK change had a counter-intuitive negative effect at high concurrency:
154	
155	- p50 unchanged (0.0%), indicating median behavior is dominated by the sequential IPFS pin operations (steps 1, 4, 5) which were not parallelized
156	- p95 increased by +138.5% (18.7s to 44.7s) -- concurrent metadata pin + IPNS publish doubled the simultaneous write load on flatfs, causing severe contention at the tail
157	- Throughput dropped -26.4% (3.45 to 2.54 ops/s) -- the increased tail latency held up client slots, reducing overall throughput
158	- Total test duration increased 36% (290s to 394s)
159	
160	**Conclusion:** Concurrent SDK pins without a matching datastore improvement creates more write contention than it saves in sequential wait time, especially under high concurrency where flatfs's file-per-block storage becomes an I/O bottleneck.
161	
162	**Pebbleds datastore (Run 3 vs Run 2): RESCUED performance and pushed past baseline.**
163	
164	Switching from flatfs to pebbleds while keeping concurrent SDK pins active produced dramatic improvements:
165	
166	- p95 dropped -63.5% (44.7s to 16.3s) -- pebbleds' LSM-tree batched writes absorbed the concurrent pin load that overwhelmed flatfs
167	- p99 dropped -65.3% (50.3s to 17.5s) -- near-elimination of the extreme tail latency caused by flatfs contention
168	- Throughput increased +45.3% (2.54 to 3.69 ops/s) -- the fastest of all three runs
169	
170	**Combined effect (Run 3 vs Run 1): The optimizations are synergistic, not additive.**
171	
172	- p50 reduced -5.5% (14,664ms to 13,860ms) -- modest median improvement
173	- p95 reduced -13.0% (18,734ms to 16,302ms) -- meaningful tail improvement
174	- p99 reduced -14.9% (20,519ms to 17,467ms) -- consistent tail improvement
175	- Throughput improved +7.0% (3.45 to 3.69 ops/s)
176	
177	The key finding is that **SDK concurrent pins REQUIRE pebbleds to deliver any benefit**. The two optimizations exhibit a mandatory synergy: concurrent pins generate more simultaneous write I/O, and only pebbleds (with its batched LSM writes) can handle that load without contention-induced tail blow-up. Deploying concurrent pins without pebbleds would be a performance regression.
178	
179	### Definitive Success Criteria Analysis (Three-Point)
180	
181	This section provides the definitive SC analysis using matched-environment data. The earlier staging-vs-local comparison above was preliminary and confounded by environment and client-count mismatches.
182	
183	#### SC1: Per-upload server time reduced to ~3.5s p50 (from ~5.4s)
184	
185	**NOT MET at 50 clients -- but target was based on different conditions.** The three-point comparison at 50 clients shows p50 of 13.9s (Run 3) vs 14.7s (Run 1), a 5.5% improvement. The original ~5.4s figure came from Prometheus server-side measurements at lower concurrency on staging. At 50 concurrent clients, per-upload time is dominated by queueing and resource contention, not the sequential API call chain.
186	
187	For reference, the concurrency probe shows p50 at 1 client = 131ms and at 5 clients = 1,016ms, both well below the 3.5s target. The SC1 target is achievable at lower concurrency levels. At high concurrency (50 clients), the bottleneck shifts from sequential API calls to IPFS infrastructure throughput, which both optimizations address at the tail (p95/p99) rather than the median.
188	
189	#### SC2: 50-client scaling behavior
190	
191	**OBSERVABLE from the concurrency probe.** The probe shows clear scaling behavior:
192	
193	| Clients | p50      | Throughput | p50 per additional client |
194	| ------- | -------- | ---------- | ------------------------- |
195	| 1       | 131ms    | 6.36 ops/s | --                        |
196	| 5       | 1,016ms  | 4.97 ops/s | +221ms/client             |
197	| 10      | 2,499ms  | 3.95 ops/s | +297ms/client             |
198	| 20      | 5,897ms  | 3.43 ops/s | +340ms/client             |
199	| 50      | 14,789ms | 3.36 ops/s | +296ms/client             |
200	
201	Throughput degrades gracefully from 6.36 ops/s (1 client) to 3.36 ops/s (50 clients) -- a 47% reduction over a 50x increase in concurrency. The system remains stable with zero errors up to 50 clients. At 75 clients, errors begin appearing, establishing the local infrastructure ceiling. With pebbleds, 50-client throughput improves to 3.69 ops/s (Run 3), indicating better scaling under load.
202	
203	#### SC3: >15% throughput increase at matched client count
204	
205	**NOT MET.** The three-point comparison at 50 clients shows +7.0% throughput improvement (3.45 to 3.69 ops/s). While the improvement is consistent and error-free, it falls short of the 15% target.
206	
207	However, the improvement is entirely attributable to the pebbleds datastore. SDK concurrent pins alone caused a -26.4% regression. The +7.0% combined improvement represents the net effect after pebbleds overcomes the concurrent-pins contention penalty and adds its own I/O efficiency gains.
208	
209	The tail latency improvements are more substantial: p95 -13.0%, p99 -14.9%. The optimizations provide more benefit at the tail than at the median, which is valuable for user experience (fewer slow outliers) even if median throughput improvement is modest.
210	
211	#### SC4: Before/after documented with matched environment
212	
213	**MET.** This three-point local comparison section provides the definitive matched-environment before/after analysis. All three runs used identical infrastructure (localhost API, <docker-host> Docker host, someguy routing), identical client count (50), and identical test scenario (upload-throughput, 20 files per client, 1KB-500KB). The only variables changed between runs were SDK mode and datastore type.
214	
215	## Success Criteria Analysis (Preliminary)
216	
217	> **Note:** The analysis below was the original preliminary assessment using mismatched environments (staging vs local) and client counts (10 vs 5). See the "Definitive Success Criteria Analysis (Three-Point)" section above for the authoritative assessment.

219	### SC1: Per-upload server time reduced to ~3.5s p50 (from ~5.4s)
220	
221	**Likely MET but requires staging Prometheus validation.** The client-side p50 of 1.5s at 5 clients is significantly below the target. However, the pre-optimization 5.4s figure was measured server-side via Prometheus histograms on staging under higher concurrency (10-200 clients). A true apples-to-apples comparison requires running the same Prometheus analysis on staging with pebbleds deployed.
222	
223	The 1.5s client-side p50 at 5 clients includes:
224	
225	- Network round-trips (localhost, minimal)
226	- Client-side encryption
227	- All 5 API calls (now with steps 2+3 concurrent)
228	
229	This is consistent with the optimization removing ~1.7s from the sequential path.
230	
231	### SC3: >15% throughput increase at 5 clients
232	
233	**Cannot be validated with current data.** The pre-optimization baseline used 10 clients on staging (5.87 ops/s) and the post-optimization used 5 clients on localhost (3.12 ops/s). These are not comparable due to:
234	
235	1. Different client counts (throughput scales with clients)
236	2. Different environments (staging VPS vs local)
237	3. Different rate limiting configurations
238	
239	**SC3 validation requires:** Running load tests on staging after pebbleds deployment, using the same client count and environment.
240	
241	### SC2 & SC4: Deferred to Staging
242	
243	- SC2 (50-client scaling) requires staging environment with relaxed rate limits
244	- SC4 (Prometheus histograms) requires staging Grafana dashboards
245	
246	## Caveats
247	
248	1. **Environment mismatch (preliminary comparison):** Pre-optimization baselines from staging; post-optimization from local. Direct percentage comparisons are indicative, not definitive. The three-point local comparison above resolves this.
249	2. **Client count mismatch (preliminary comparison):** Pre-optimization upload test used 10 clients; post-optimization used 5. Throughput is not directly comparable. The three-point comparison uses 50 clients consistently.
250	3. **Mixed workload invalid:** 100% error rate in post-optimization mixed workload run makes that data unsuitable for comparison. Root cause likely rate limiting or SDK concurrent operation conflicts under mixed workload patterns.
251	4. **Rate limiting:** Local API running in development mode (not NODE_ENV=test) applies tighter rate limits, causing 429 errors at 10 clients. The 5-client upload test completed cleanly. Three-point runs used NODE_ENV=test with bypass secrets.
252	5. **Concurrent pins + flatfs regression:** SDK concurrent pins without pebbleds cause a performance regression at 50 clients. Both optimizations must be deployed together.
253	6. **SC3 not met at 50 clients:** Throughput improvement is +7.0%, below the 15% target. Tail latency improvements (p95 -13.0%, p99 -14.9%) are more substantial.
254

256	
257	To test whether pebbleds extends the infrastructure's concurrency ceiling, a bonus run was performed at 75 clients — the level where the flatfs probe failed with 10 errors and a 600s timeout.

# Performance Baselines - Phase 19.2 (POST-Optimization)

> These are POST-optimization baselines. Kubo datastore: pebbleds (LSM-tree). SDK upload flow: concurrent pins (Promise.allSettled for steps 2+3).

## Capture Information

Move, rename, and delete operations were skipped because they require previously created items which failed. This makes the mixed workload data unreliable for comparison -- see Caveats section below.

## Before/After Comparison

### Environment Caveat

The pre-optimization baselines were captured against **staging** infrastructure (api-staging.cipherbox.cc, warm DHT, 4 vCPU VPS) while post-optimization baselines were captured against **local** infrastructure (localhost API, <docker-host> Docker host). These are different environments with different network characteristics, so percentage changes must be interpreted with caution.

Additionally, the pre-optimization upload test used **10 clients** while this post-optimization test used **5 clients** (as specified in plan). More clients increases contention and latency, which means the pre-optimization numbers at 10 clients would be higher than at 5 clients.

### Upload Throughput Comparison (primary metric)

| Metric             | Pre-Optimization (staging, 10 clients) | Post-Optimization (local, 5 clients) | Change | Notes                               |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ------ | ----------------------------------- |
| uploadFile p50     | 1,442ms                                | 1,502ms                              | +4.2%  | Within noise given environment diff |
| uploadFile p95     | 3,666ms                                | 2,841ms                              | -22.5% | Significant improvement at tail     |
| uploadFile p99     | 4,044ms                                | 3,432ms                              | -15.1% | Tail latency reduced                |
| uploadFile avg     | 1,649ms                                | 1,613ms                              | -2.2%  | Essentially flat                    |
| throughput (ops/s) | 5.87                                   | 3.12                                 | -46.8% | NOT comparable: 10 vs 5 clients     |
| errors             | 0                                      | 0                                    | --     | Both error-free                     |

### Mixed Workload Comparison (limited validity)

| Metric           | Pre-Optimization (staging, 5 clients) | Post-Optimization (local, 5 clients) | Change | Notes                                  |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ------ | -------------------------------------- |
| createFolder p50 | 511ms                                 | 500ms                                | -2.2%  | Similar                                |
| uploadFile p50   | 613ms                                 | 892ms                                | +45.5% | Post-opt data unreliable (all errored) |
| mixed throughput | 9.32 ops/s                            | 5.72 ops/s                           | -38.6% | Post-opt data unreliable (all errored) |

**Mixed workload comparison is NOT valid:** The post-optimization run had 100% error rate across all operations, meaning the latency numbers reflect error-path timing (fast failures), not successful operation timing. The pre-optimization mixed workload numbers came from staging with zero errors.

### Server-Side Latency Analysis

From the pre-optimization Prometheus data, a single `uploadFile` makes 5 sequential API calls totaling ~5.4s server-side:

| Step      | API Call                        | Pre-Optimization | Expected Post-Optimization | Optimization Applied        |
| --------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------- | -------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| 1         | POST /ipfs/upload (ciphertext)  | 1.73s            | 1.73s (unchanged)          | pebbleds may reduce         |
| 2         | POST /ipfs/upload (metadata)    | 1.73s            | Concurrent with step 3     | SDK concurrent pins         |
| 3         | POST /ipns/publish-batch        | 0.11s            | Concurrent with step 2     | SDK concurrent pins         |
| 4         | POST /ipfs/upload (folder meta) | 1.73s            | 1.73s (unchanged)          | pebbleds may reduce         |
| 5         | POST /ipns/publish              | 0.14s            | 0.14s (unchanged)          | None                        |
| **Total** |                                 | **~5.4s**        | **~3.7s expected**         | Save ~1.7s from concurrency |

The observed p50 of 1.5s (5 clients, local) is well below the pre-optimization server-side estimate of 5.4s. This confirms that both optimizations (concurrent pins + pebbleds) are contributing to reduced per-upload latency.

## Three-Point Local Comparison (Matched Environment)

### Methodology

All three measurement runs used the same local environment: API on localhost:3000, Docker services (IPFS/Kubo v0.40.0, PostgreSQL, Redis, someguy) on <docker-host> with someguy delegated routing (<docker-host>:8190). Each run used 50 concurrent clients uploading 20 files each (1KB-500KB random sizes, 1,000 total operations). The 50-client count was determined by a concurrency probe (Run 0) as the highest stable count with zero errors. Each run isolates one optimization variable:

- **Run 1 (No Opts):** Sequential SDK upload flow + flatfs datastore (pre-optimization baseline)
- **Run 2 (SDK Concurrent):** Concurrent SDK pins (Promise.allSettled for steps 2+3) + flatfs datastore
- **Run 3 (SDK + Pebbleds):** Concurrent SDK pins + pebbleds datastore (LSM-tree)

Rate limit bypass was applied to all runs (LOAD_TEST_SECRET + THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET passed inline, API running with NODE_ENV=test).

### Concurrency Probe (Run 0)

Before the three-point comparison, a concurrency probe established the local infrastructure's concurrency ceiling using the sequential SDK + flatfs configuration:

| Clients | uploadFile p50 | p95      | p99      | throughput ops/s | errors         |
| ------- | -------------- | -------- | -------- | ---------------- | -------------- |
| 1       | 131ms          | 287ms    | 497ms    | 6.36             | 0              |
| 5       | 1,016ms        | 1,871ms  | 2,148ms  | 4.97             | 0              |
| 10      | 2,499ms        | 3,768ms  | 4,496ms  | 3.95             | 0              |
| 20      | 5,897ms        | 8,806ms  | 9,741ms  | 3.43             | 0              |
| 50      | 14,789ms       | 19,315ms | 21,861ms | 3.36             | 0              |
| 75      | 30,804ms       | 53,603ms | 59,892ms | 2.44             | 10             |
| 100     | --             | --       | --       | --               | many (timeout) |

**Chosen N: 50 clients** -- the highest client count with zero errors and no timeout failures. At 75 clients, 10 errors appeared; at 100 clients, widespread timeouts occurred. The 50-client count also satisfies SC3's requirement to measure throughput at scale.

### Three-Point Results Table (50 clients x 20 files = 1,000 uploads)

| Metric           | Run 1 (No Opts) | Run 2 (SDK Concurrent) | Run 3 (SDK + Pebbleds) | SDK Delta (R2 vs R1) | Pebbleds Delta (R3 vs R2) | Total Delta (R3 vs R1) |
| ---------------- | --------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| uploadFile p50   | 14,664ms        | 14,664ms               | 13,860ms               | 0.0%                 | -5.5%                     | **-5.5%**              |
| uploadFile p95   | 18,734ms        | 44,704ms               | 16,302ms               | +138.5%              | -63.5%                    | **-13.0%**             |
| uploadFile p99   | 20,519ms        | 50,301ms               | 17,467ms               | +145.1%              | -65.3%                    | **-14.9%**             |
| uploadFile avg   | 14,791ms        | 20,061ms               | 13,984ms               | +35.6%               | -30.3%                    | **-5.5%**              |
| uploadFile min   | 5,463ms         | 7,194ms                | 5,453ms                | +31.7%               | -24.2%                    | -0.2%                  |
| uploadFile max   | 22,379ms        | 53,422ms               | 19,466ms               | +138.7%              | -63.6%                    | -13.0%                 |
| throughput ops/s | 3.45            | 2.54                   | 3.69                   | -26.4%               | +45.3%                    | **+7.0%**              |
| total duration   | 289.8s          | 394.0s                 | 271.1s                 | +35.9%               | -31.2%                    | -6.5%                  |
| data transferred | 250.2 MB        | 246.3 MB               | 244.7 MB               | --                   | --                        | --                     |
| errors           | 0               | 0                      | 0                      | --                   | --                        | --                     |
| datastore        | flatfs          | flatfs                 | pebbleds               | --                   | --                        | --                     |
| SDK mode         | sequential      | concurrent             | concurrent             | --                   | --                        | --                     |

### Optimization Attribution

**SDK concurrent pins alone (Run 2 vs Run 1): DEGRADED performance at 50 clients.**

The concurrent SDK change had a counter-intuitive negative effect at high concurrency:

- p50 unchanged (0.0%), indicating median behavior is dominated by the sequential IPFS pin operations (steps 1, 4, 5) which were not parallelized
- p95 increased by +138.5% (18.7s to 44.7s) -- concurrent metadata pin + IPNS publish doubled the simultaneous write load on flatfs, causing severe contention at the tail
- Throughput dropped -26.4% (3.45 to 2.54 ops/s) -- the increased tail latency held up client slots, reducing overall throughput
- Total test duration increased 36% (290s to 394s)

**Conclusion:** Concurrent SDK pins without a matching datastore improvement creates more write contention than it saves in sequential wait time, especially under high concurrency where flatfs's file-per-block storage becomes an I/O bottleneck.

**Pebbleds datastore (Run 3 vs Run 2): RESCUED performance and pushed past baseline.**

Switching from flatfs to pebbleds while keeping concurrent SDK pins active produced dramatic improvements:

- p95 dropped -63.5% (44.7s to 16.3s) -- pebbleds' LSM-tree batched writes absorbed the concurrent pin load that overwhelmed flatfs
- p99 dropped -65.3% (50.3s to 17.5s) -- near-elimination of the extreme tail latency caused by flatfs contention
- Throughput increased +45.3% (2.54 to 3.69 ops/s) -- the fastest of all three runs

**Combined effect (Run 3 vs Run 1): The optimizations are synergistic, not additive.**

- p50 reduced -5.5% (14,664ms to 13,860ms) -- modest median improvement
- p95 reduced -13.0% (18,734ms to 16,302ms) -- meaningful tail improvement
- p99 reduced -14.9% (20,519ms to 17,467ms) -- consistent tail improvement
- Throughput improved +7.0% (3.45 to 3.69 ops/s)

The key finding is that **SDK concurrent pins REQUIRE pebbleds to deliver any benefit**. The two optimizations exhibit a mandatory synergy: concurrent pins generate more simultaneous write I/O, and only pebbleds (with its batched LSM writes) can handle that load without contention-induced tail blow-up. Deploying concurrent pins without pebbleds would be a performance regression.

### Definitive Success Criteria Analysis (Three-Point)

This section provides the definitive SC analysis using matched-environment data. The earlier staging-vs-local comparison above was preliminary and confounded by environment and client-count mismatches.

#### SC1: Per-upload server time reduced to ~3.5s p50 (from ~5.4s)

**NOT MET at 50 clients -- but target was based on different conditions.** The three-point comparison at 50 clients shows p50 of 13.9s (Run 3) vs 14.7s (Run 1), a 5.5% improvement. The original ~5.4s figure came from Prometheus server-side measurements at lower concurrency on staging. At 50 concurrent clients, per-upload time is dominated by queueing and resource contention, not the sequential API call chain.

For reference, the concurrency probe shows p50 at 1 client = 131ms and at 5 clients = 1,016ms, both well below the 3.5s target. The SC1 target is achievable at lower concurrency levels. At high concurrency (50 clients), the bottleneck shifts from sequential API calls to IPFS infrastructure throughput, which both optimizations address at the tail (p95/p99) rather than the median.

#### SC2: 50-client scaling behavior

**OBSERVABLE from the concurrency probe.** The probe shows clear scaling behavior:

| Clients | p50      | Throughput | p50 per additional client |
| ------- | -------- | ---------- | ------------------------- |
| 1       | 131ms    | 6.36 ops/s | --                        |
| 5       | 1,016ms  | 4.97 ops/s | +221ms/client             |
| 10      | 2,499ms  | 3.95 ops/s | +297ms/client             |
| 20      | 5,897ms  | 3.43 ops/s | +340ms/client             |
| 50      | 14,789ms | 3.36 ops/s | +296ms/client             |

Throughput degrades gracefully from 6.36 ops/s (1 client) to 3.36 ops/s (50 clients) -- a 47% reduction over a 50x increase in concurrency. The system remains stable with zero errors up to 50 clients. At 75 clients, errors begin appearing, establishing the local infrastructure ceiling. With pebbleds, 50-client throughput improves to 3.69 ops/s (Run 3), indicating better scaling under load.

#### SC3: >15% throughput increase at matched client count

**NOT MET.** The three-point comparison at 50 clients shows +7.0% throughput improvement (3.45 to 3.69 ops/s). While the improvement is consistent and error-free, it falls short of the 15% target.

However, the improvement is entirely attributable to the pebbleds datastore. SDK concurrent pins alone caused a -26.4% regression. The +7.0% combined improvement represents the net effect after pebbleds overcomes the concurrent-pins contention penalty and adds its own I/O efficiency gains.

The tail latency improvements are more substantial: p95 -13.0%, p99 -14.9%. The optimizations provide more benefit at the tail than at the median, which is valuable for user experience (fewer slow outliers) even if median throughput improvement is modest.

#### SC4: Before/after documented with matched environment

**MET.** This three-point local comparison section provides the definitive matched-environment before/after analysis. All three runs used identical infrastructure (localhost API, <docker-host> Docker host, someguy routing), identical client count (50), and identical test scenario (upload-throughput, 20 files per client, 1KB-500KB). The only variables changed between runs were SDK mode and datastore type.

## Success Criteria Analysis (Preliminary)

> **Note:** The analysis below was the original preliminary assessment using mismatched environments (staging vs local) and client counts (10 vs 5). See the "Definitive Success Criteria Analysis (Three-Point)" section above for the authoritative assessment.

### SC1: Per-upload server time reduced to ~3.5s p50 (from ~5.4s)

**Likely MET but requires staging Prometheus validation.** The client-side p50 of 1.5s at 5 clients is significantly below the target. However, the pre-optimization 5.4s figure was measured server-side via Prometheus histograms on staging under higher concurrency (10-200 clients). A true apples-to-apples comparison requires running the same Prometheus analysis on staging with pebbleds deployed.

The 1.5s client-side p50 at 5 clients includes:

- Network round-trips (localhost, minimal)
- Client-side encryption
- All 5 API calls (now with steps 2+3 concurrent)

This is consistent with the optimization removing ~1.7s from the sequential path.

### SC3: >15% throughput increase at 5 clients

**Cannot be validated with current data.** The pre-optimization baseline used 10 clients on staging (5.87 ops/s) and the post-optimization used 5 clients on localhost (3.12 ops/s). These are not comparable due to:

1. Different client counts (throughput scales with clients)
2. Different environments (staging VPS vs local)
3. Different rate limiting configurations

**SC3 validation requires:** Running load tests on staging after pebbleds deployment, using the same client count and environment.

### SC2 & SC4: Deferred to Staging

- SC2 (50-client scaling) requires staging environment with relaxed rate limits
- SC4 (Prometheus histograms) requires staging Grafana dashboards

## Caveats

1. **Environment mismatch (preliminary comparison):** Pre-optimization baselines from staging; post-optimization from local. Direct percentage comparisons are indicative, not definitive. The three-point local comparison above resolves this.
2. **Client count mismatch (preliminary comparison):** Pre-optimization upload test used 10 clients; post-optimization used 5. Throughput is not directly comparable. The three-point comparison uses 50 clients consistently.
3. **Mixed workload invalid:** 100% error rate in post-optimization mixed workload run makes that data unsuitable for comparison. Root cause likely rate limiting or SDK concurrent operation conflicts under mixed workload patterns.
4. **Rate limiting:** Local API running in development mode (not NODE_ENV=test) applies tighter rate limits, causing 429 errors at 10 clients. The 5-client upload test completed cleanly. Three-point runs used NODE_ENV=test with bypass secrets.
5. **Concurrent pins + flatfs regression:** SDK concurrent pins without pebbleds cause a performance regression at 50 clients. Both optimizations must be deployed together.
6. **SC3 not met at 50 clients:** Throughput improvement is +7.0%, below the 15% target. Tail latency improvements (p95 -13.0%, p99 -14.9%) are more substantial.

## 75-Client Stress Test (Bonus Run)

To test whether pebbleds extends the infrastructure's concurrency ceiling, a bonus run was performed at 75 clients — the level where the flatfs probe failed with 10 errors and a 600s timeout.

| Metric           | 75 clients (sequential + flatfs, probe) | 75 clients (concurrent + pebbleds, bonus) | Change         |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | -------------- |
| uploadFile p50   | 30,804ms                                | 21,969ms                                  | **-28.7%**     |
| uploadFile p95   | 53,603ms                                | 25,316ms                                  | **-52.8%**     |
| uploadFile p99   | 59,892ms                                | 26,879ms                                  | **-55.1%**     |
| uploadFile avg   | 32,354ms                                | 21,901ms                                  | **-32.3%**     |
| throughput ops/s | 2.44                                    | 3.51                                      | **+43.9%**     |
| errors           | 10                                      | **0**                                     | **eliminated** |
| status           | timed out (600s)                        | **clean (427s)**                          | **fixed**      |

**Key finding:** Pebbleds doesn't just improve performance at high concurrency — it eliminates the failure mode entirely. At 75 clients, flatfs produced auth token expiry cascades (401s → "Key wrapping failed" → "Folder not loaded"), while pebbleds completed all 1500 ops with zero errors. The throughput improvement of +43.9% at 75 clients far exceeds the +7.0% seen at 50 clients, suggesting pebbleds' benefits scale with concurrency pressure.

This result also satisfies **SC3 (>15% throughput improvement)** at the 75-client level, even though it was not met at 50 clients.

## Staging CI Load Tests (Post-Deploy, Matched Environment)

Post-deploy staging baselines captured via GitHub Actions CI runner (`Load Tests` workflow) against `api-staging.cipherbox.cc`. These are directly comparable to the pre-19.2 staging baselines which used the same CI runner, same workflow, same staging VPS hardware.

**Environment:** GitHub Actions runner → staging VPS (76.13.151.200), Kubo v0.40.0 with pebbleds, SDK with concurrent pins (Promise.allSettled).

### vs Pre-19.2 Staging Baselines

- System broke at ~200 concurrent clients

Found it. Here's the full picture.

## The load test: `.github/workflows/load-test.yml` ("Load Tests")

Manual-dispatch-only workflow that runs the `tests/load/` vitest scenarios against a **live** API target. Two targets: `local` (spins up Postgres/Kubo/Redis + API as services) or `staging` (hits the deployed `STAGING_API_URL`).

**Where it was built** — the instrumentation you're remembering came in across these phases:
- **Phase 18** (`performance-instrumentation`) — Prometheus histograms + first staging baselines
- **Phase 19.2** (`ipfs-upload-performance-optimization`) — pebbleds datastore, the staging CI load-test scaling tables
- **Phase 21** (`byo-ipfs-node-support`) — the `byo-*` scenarios
- **Phase 22** (`performance-baselines-completion`) + **Phase 34** (`e2e-test-expansion-staging-baselines`) — baseline completion

## How to fire it against staging

Code under test = whatever is **deployed** to staging (target is `STAGING_API_URL`), not the workflow ref. So **run it after your deploy lands**, otherwise you'll measure the old build. Dispatch from `main`:

```bash
env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh workflow run load-test.yml \
  -f environment=staging \
  -f scenario=upload-throughput \
  -f client_count=200
```

Staging secrets/vars are already wired (`STAGING_API_URL`, `STAGING_TEST_LOGIN_SECRET`, `STAGING_THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET`) and it runs under the `staging` GitHub environment — **the run may pause for environment approval**.

**Critical gotcha** (from `.learnings/2026-03-29-staging-load-test-throttle-bypass.md`): never run two staging scenarios concurrently — combined load saturates the 4-vCPU VPS and you get false 429s. The workflow's `concurrency: load-test-staging` + `cancel-in-progress: false` enforces queueing, so just dispatch them one at a time.

## What to compare against (regression anchors)

| Scenario | Anchor | Key baseline numbers |
|---|---|---|
| `upload-throughput` @ 50/100/200 | 19.2 staging CI table | **15.10 / 18.76 / 19.22 ops/s**, 0/0/58 errors |
| `sustained-load` @ 200 | `tests/load/baselines/staging-sustained-load.json` (2026-03-29) | uploadFile p95 **11.6s**, createFolder p95 **11.9s**, 0.17% error rate |
| `byo-capacity-ceiling` | `staging-byo-capacity-ceiling.json` | ⚠️ all-error (Pinata free-tier quota exhausted) — **skip, not useful for regression** |

Pass/fail thresholds (`tests/load/src/harness/thresholds.ts`): the run **fails** if `uploadFile p95 > 10s` or `createFolder p95 > 5s` — note the existing sustained-load baseline already trips both at 200 clients, so a 200-client run is expected to "fail" the threshold gate; judge by the metrics artifact (`metrics-*.json`, retained 30 days), not the green/red.

## Recommendation

Best signal for "did recent API changes regress perf" is **`upload-throughput` at matched 50 / 100 / 200 clients** vs the 19.2 staging table — same workflow, same VPS, directly comparable. Then `sustained-load` @ 200 vs the March baseline. Run them sequentially.

Checked the actual scenario code. Your instinct is right to ask — but the premise is already handled: **these scenarios go through the SDK, not raw endpoints.** Here's exactly what hits the wire.

## What surface each scenario uses

The pool (`client-pool.ts:70`) provisions **real accounts** via `createTestAccount` (the full 5-step sdk-e2e flow) — each virtual client is a genuine authenticated `CipherBoxClient` with its own vault, root IPNS keypair, and folder key. Then the workloads drive the **high-level SDK client methods**, same surface the desktop/web app uses:

- **`upload-throughput`** → `runFileWorkload` calls `client.uploadFile(...)` (`client.ts:1005`). One "uploadFile" metric is **not** a raw `POST /ipfs/upload` — it fans out to the whole real-user pipeline: encrypt → pin ciphertext → pin file metadata → `Promise.allSettled([batchPublishIpnsRecords, updateFolderMetadataAndPublish])` → folder-meta pin + folder IPNS publish. ~4–5 endpoints incl. the IPNS publish bottleneck. The scenario comment says it outright: *"including IPNS publish per file."*
- **`mixed-workload`** → `client.createFolder / uploadFile / renameItem / moveItem / deleteItem` with weighted-random mix (4:2:1:1:1) and live folder-tree state. **This is the "bunch of real users doing realistic things" simulation you're describing.**
- **`sustained-load`** → steady 2 ops/sec/client of create→upload→delete for 300s — catches leaks / connection-pool exhaustion / time-based degradation.

So the SDK-driven real-user simulation already exists and is what's dispatchable against staging.

## Where you're actually right — two real gaps

1. **It's write-path-heavy.** `upload-throughput` sets `verifyDownloads: false`, and the dispatchable set barely exercises **reads** (resolve/fetch/decrypt), versioning, or sharing. If your recent API changes touched read or share paths, none of the staging-dispatchable scenarios will catch a regression there.

2. **The single-surface isolation scenarios aren't wired to staging.** There's a second family — `sdk-upload-pipeline`, `sdk-folder-read`, `sdk-ipns-contention` — that calls `sdk-core` functions **directly** (`sdkCore.uploadFile`, `createAndPublishIpnsRecord`, `loadFolderMetadata`), bypassing `CipherBoxClient` to isolate one bottleneck (e.g. pure read path, pure IPNS contention). These are **not in the workflow's `scenario` dropdown** — only the 5 non-byo + 3 byo are. To run them against staging you'd add the name to the `choice` list (one-line edit; vitest matches by filename substring) or run locally with `LOAD_TEST_API_URL` pointed at staging.

## Recommendation

For "did recent API changes regress perf across realistic usage," run this trio sequentially against staging (per the no-concurrent-runs rule):

1. **`mixed-workload`** @ 50/100/200 — realistic CRUD mix (the real-user sim)
2. **`sustained-load`** @ 200 — steady-state; compare directly to `staging-sustained-load.json` (uploadFile p95 11.6s, createFolder p95 11.9s, 0.17% errors)
3. **`upload-throughput`** @ 50/100/200 — write-path number vs the 19.2 staging CI table (15.10/18.76/19.22 ops/s)

# Sequential staging load-test sweep.
# Dispatches load-test.yml runs one at a time (never concurrent -> respects the
# "no concurrent staging load tests" rule), polls each to completion, and
# downloads its metrics artifact. NOT committed; scratch tooling for a one-off sweep.
set -uo pipefail

REPO="FSM1/cipher-box"
WF_FILE="load-test.yml"
WF_ID="249928808"
OUTDIR="${1:?usage: staging-loadtest-sweep.sh <outdir>}"
LOG="$OUTDIR/progress.log"
SUMMARY="$OUTDIR/summary.tsv"
mkdir -p "$OUTDIR"

log() { echo "[$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)] $*" | tee -a "$LOG"; }
gh_retry() { local i; for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh "$@" 2>>"$LOG" && return 0; sleep 5; done; return 1; }

runs=(
  "mixed-workload:50"
  "mixed-workload:100"
  "mixed-workload:200"
  "sustained-load:200"
  "upload-throughput:50"
  "upload-throughput:100"
  "upload-throughput:200"
)

printf 'scenario\tclients\trun_id\tconclusion\tartifact_dir\n' > "$SUMMARY"
log "=== Staging load-test sweep: ${#runs[@]} runs against $REPO ==="

for spec in "${runs[@]}"; do
  scenario="${spec%%:*}"; clients="${spec##*:}"
  label="$scenario @ ${clients} clients"
  log "--- Dispatching: $label ---"

  before="$(gh_retry api "repos/$REPO/actions/workflows/$WF_ID/runs?per_page=1" --jq '.workflow_runs[0].id' || echo 0)"

  if ! gh_retry workflow run "$WF_FILE" -f environment=staging -f scenario="$scenario" -f client_count="$clients"; then
    log "!! DISPATCH FAILED for $label -- skipping"
    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$scenario" "$clients" "-" "dispatch_failed" "-" >> "$SUMMARY"
    continue
  fi

  runid=""
  for _ in $(seq 1 36); do
    sleep 5
    latest="$(gh_retry api "repos/$REPO/actions/workflows/$WF_ID/runs?per_page=1" --jq '.workflow_runs[0].id' || echo 0)"
    if [ "$latest" != "$before" ] && [ "$latest" != "0" ]; then runid="$latest"; break; fi
  done
  if [ -z "$runid" ]; then
    log "!! Could not capture run id for $label -- skipping"
    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$scenario" "$clients" "-" "no_run_id" "-" >> "$SUMMARY"
    continue
  fi
  log "Run id $runid ($label) -> https://github.com/$REPO/actions/runs/$runid"

  status="queued"
  while [ "$status" != "completed" ]; do
    sleep 20
    status="$(gh_retry api "repos/$REPO/actions/runs/$runid" --jq '.status' || echo unknown)"
  done
  concl="$(gh_retry api "repos/$REPO/actions/runs/$runid" --jq '.conclusion' || echo unknown)"
  log "Run $runid completed: conclusion=$concl"

  rundir="$OUTDIR/${scenario}-${clients}c"
  mkdir -p "$rundir"
  if gh_retry run download "$runid" -R "$REPO" -D "$rundir"; then
    log "Artifacts -> $rundir"
  else
    log "No artifact downloaded for $label (conclusion=$concl)"
  fi
  printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$scenario" "$clients" "$runid" "$concl" "$rundir" >> "$SUMMARY"
done

log "=== SWEEP COMPLETE ==="

Got the numbers. **That "failure" is a 34 ms overshoot on an arbitrary threshold with zero errors — not a regression signal.**

Mixed-workload @ 50 clients (2,177 ops, **0 errors**):

| Op | count | p50 | p95 | p99 | throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| createFolder | 541 | 3,131ms | **5,034ms** ⟵ trips 5,000 gate | 5,591ms | 3.32/s |
| uploadFile | 1,003 | 4,147ms | 5,857ms | 6,767ms | 6.15/s |
| **moveItem** | 207 | 6,523ms | **9,142ms** | 10,393ms | 1.27/s |
| renameItem | 205 | 1,372ms | 3,074ms | 3,634ms | 1.26/s |
| deleteItem | 221 | 1,344ms | 3,133ms | 3,633ms | 1.35/s |

**Root cause:** createFolder p95 came in at 5,034ms vs the hardcoded 5,000ms gate — **0.7% over**, zero errors, zero timeouts. createFolder is IPNS-publish-bound, and at 50 concurrent clients on the 4-vCPU staging VPS that publish queue pushes p95 right to ~5s. The March anchor confirms the scaling curve: createFolder p95 was 11.9s at 200 clients, so ~5s at 50 is exactly on-trend. The gate is mis-calibrated for 50-client staging, not the API regressing. There's also no prior mixed-workload@50 staging baseline to regress *against* — this run **is** the new baseline for that config, and it's healthy.

**The actual finding worth your attention:** `moveItem` is the real tail hotspot — p95 9.1s, p99 10.4s, slower than uploadFile. That's structural (a move = two folder-metadata updates + two IPNS publishes), not necessarily a regression, but it's where the latency lives and it's currently ungated.

Two things I'll tee up for the re-baselining (not touching code mid-sweep):
1. The createFolder 5s gate should be concurrency-scaled (or relaxed for 50+ clients) — it's failing green runs on a knife-edge.
2. Add a `moveItem` threshold so the slowest real operation is actually tracked.

Sweep is proceeding normally — run 2 (`mixed-workload` @ 100) in progress. I'll hold for the full set and deliver the consolidated diff + baseline-refresh proposal at the end.

## Headline: upload throughput ~halved, latency ~doubled

`upload-throughput` is the clean apples-to-apples anchor (same workflow, same VPS, same scenario as the Phase 19.2 post-deploy staging baseline):

| Clients | Metric | 19.2 baseline | **Now (06-22)** | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 50 | throughput | 15.10/s | **7.71/s** | **−49%** |
| 50 | p50 / p95 | 3,242 / 4,615ms | **6,364 / 8,760ms** | **+96% / +90%** |

**`sustained-load` @ 200 confirms it** (vs March `staging-sustained-load.json`): ~33% fewer ops completed in the same 5-min window (11,174 → 7,479), uploadFile p95 +50% (11.6s → 17.5s), and the **p99 tail blew up** — uploadFile p99 13.2s → **55.6s** (+321%), createFolder p99 15.7s → 40.3s.

**`mixed-workload`** has no prior staging anchor (the only earlier run was 5-client local + 100% errored), so it's a fresh baseline — healthy error-wise (0/1/16 errors at 50/100/200) but it surfaced one pathology: **`moveItem` degrades super-linearly** — p95 9.1s → **42.3s** going from 50→100 clients. A move = two folder-metadata updates + two IPNS publishes, and that doubles down hard under contention. It's currently ungated.

## Most likely root cause — check this first

The magnitude is the tell: **~2× slower upload almost exactly matches the documented Phase 19.2 flatfs→pebbleds delta.** The strongest hypothesis is that **staging's Kubo datastore is no longer on the `pebbleds` profile** — a redeploy that reset `IPFS_PROFILE` to the default `flatfs` would reproduce this regression on its own, with zero code changes. That's the single highest-probability cause given how cleanly the numbers line up.

To confirm and split infra-vs-code, I'd:
1. **Check staging Kubo datastore** — `ipfs config Datastore.Spec.type` on the staging VPS (should be `pebbleds`; if it's `flatfs`, that's almost certainly the whole story).
2. **Pull staging Prometheus histograms** (`cipherbox_ipfs_*_duration_seconds`) — if server-side pin/publish latency doubled, it's infra; if it's flat, the added latency is in the client-side SDK path (e.g. the newer `selectEncryptionMode`/pipeline changes running on the runner).

## Next steps — pick one

The full per-op metrics are saved under `loadtest-staging-2026-06-22/` (scratch, uncommitted).

Want me to:
- **(a) Investigate the root cause** — SSH to staging (1Password agent) to check the datastore profile + pull `/metrics`, and report back whether this is infra or code? *(recommended — cheap, and likely conclusive)*
- **(b) Persist these as the fresh staging baselines** — write the 7 runs into `tests/load/baselines/` + a dated `.planning/baselines/` doc so the next round has a current anchor?
- **(c) Fix the threshold calibration** — concurrency-scale the createFolder gate and add a `moveItem` gate so green runs stop failing on knife-edges and the real hotspot gets tracked?

My call: **(a) first** — no point re-baselining a number that's 2× off if a one-line `IPFS_PROFILE` fix restores it.

458	      - name: Copy files to VPS
459	        uses: appleboy/scp-action@ff85246acaad7bdce478db94a363cd2bf7c90345 # v1.0.0

531	            docker compose -f docker-compose.staging.yml restart caddy
532	
533	            # Cleanup old images

538	    needs: [deploy-vps]
539	    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
540	    environment: staging
541	    permissions:
542	      contents: read
543	    steps:
544	      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
545	        with:
546	          ref: ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}
547	
548	      - name: Wait for Grafana Cloud readiness
549	        env:
550	          GRAFANA_URL: ${{ vars.GRAFANA_URL }}
551	          GRAFANA_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GRAFANA_API_KEY }}
552	        run: |
553	          set -euo pipefail
554	          : "${GRAFANA_URL:?GRAFANA_URL is required for Grafana readiness check}"
555	          : "${GRAFANA_API_KEY:?GRAFANA_API_KEY is required for Grafana readiness check}"
556	          GRAFANA_URL="${GRAFANA_URL%/}"
557	          MAX_ATTEMPTS=30
558	          INTERVAL=10
559	          for ((i=1; i<=MAX_ATTEMPTS; i++)); do
560	            HTTP_CODE=$(curl -sS --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 15 \
561	              -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" \
562	              -H "Authorization: Bearer ${GRAFANA_API_KEY}" \
563	              "${GRAFANA_URL}/api/health") || HTTP_CODE=000
564	            if [[ "$HTTP_CODE" == "200" ]]; then
565	              echo "Grafana Cloud is ready (attempt $i/$MAX_ATTEMPTS)"
566	              exit 0
567	            elif [[ "$HTTP_CODE" =~ ^(401|403|404)$ ]]; then
568	              echo "::error::Grafana returned HTTP $HTTP_CODE — check GRAFANA_URL and GRAFANA_API_KEY"
569	              exit 1
570	            fi
571	            echo "Grafana not ready (HTTP $HTTP_CODE), waiting ${INTERVAL}s... ($i/$MAX_ATTEMPTS)"
572	            sleep "$INTERVAL"
573	          done
574	          echo "::error::Grafana Cloud did not become ready after $((MAX_ATTEMPTS * INTERVAL))s"
575	          exit 1
576	
577	      - name: Push dashboard to Grafana Cloud
578	        env:
579	          GRAFANA_URL: ${{ vars.GRAFANA_URL }}
580	          GRAFANA_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GRAFANA_API_KEY }}
581	          DS_METRICS_UID: ${{ vars.GRAFANA_DS_METRICS_UID }}
582	          DS_LOGS_UID: ${{ vars.GRAFANA_DS_LOGS_UID }}
583	        run: |
584	          set -euo pipefail
585	          : "${GRAFANA_URL:?GRAFANA_URL is required}"
586	          : "${GRAFANA_API_KEY:?GRAFANA_API_KEY is required}"
587	          : "${DS_METRICS_UID:?GRAFANA_DS_METRICS_UID is required}"
588	          : "${DS_LOGS_UID:?GRAFANA_DS_LOGS_UID is required}"
589	          GRAFANA_URL="${GRAFANA_URL%/}"
590	
591	          # The dashboard JSON uses __inputs for datasource templating.
592	          # Replace variable references with actual datasource UIDs.
593	          DASHBOARD=$(cat docker/grafana/dashboards/cipherbox-staging.json \
594	            | jq --arg metrics "$DS_METRICS_UID" --arg logs "$DS_LOGS_UID" \
595	                 'del(.__inputs)
596	                  | .id = null
597	                  | walk(if type == "object" and .uid? and (.uid | test("\\$\\{DS_")) then
598	                      .uid = (if .uid == "${DS_GRAFANA_CLOUD_METRICS}" then $metrics
599	                              elif .uid == "${DS_GRAFANA_CLOUD_LOGS}" then $logs
600	                              else .uid end)
601	                    else . end)')
602	
603	          # Fail if any datasource placeholder survived the rewrite
604	          if jq -e '.. | objects | .uid? | select(type == "string" and test("^\\$\\{DS_"))' \
605	            >/dev/null <<<"$DASHBOARD"; then
606	            echo "::error::Unresolved datasource placeholder(s) remain in dashboard JSON"
607	            exit 1
608	          fi
609	
610	          # Wrap in import payload
611	          PAYLOAD=$(jq -n --argjson dashboard "$DASHBOARD" '{
612	            dashboard: $dashboard,
613	            overwrite: true,
614	            message: "Provisioned by deploy-staging workflow"
615	          }')
616	
617	          # Push to Grafana API
618	          HTTP_CODE=$(curl -sS --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 60 \
619	            -o /tmp/grafana-response.json -w "%{http_code}" \
620	            -X POST "${GRAFANA_URL}/api/dashboards/db" \
621	            -H "Authorization: Bearer ${GRAFANA_API_KEY}" \
622	            -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
623	            -d "$PAYLOAD")
624	
625	          if [[ ! "$HTTP_CODE" =~ ^2[0-9][0-9]$ ]]; then
626	            echo "::error::Grafana API returned HTTP $HTTP_CODE"
627	            cat /tmp/grafana-response.json
628	            exit 1
629	          fi
630	
631	          echo "Dashboard provisioned successfully (HTTP $HTTP_CODE)"
632	          jq -r '.url // "unknown"' /tmp/grafana-response.json
