file.content:
name: Deploy Staging

on:
  push:
    tags:
      - 'staging-*'
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      staging_tag:
        required: true
        type: string

env:
  REGISTRY: ghcr.io
  # Resolve tag: workflow_call passes it as input, push trigger uses ref_name
  DEPLOY_TAG: ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}

permissions: {}

jobs:
  build-api:
    name: Build & Push API Image
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
        with:
          ref: ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}

      - name: Set lowercase image name
        run: echo "API_IMAGE=ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER,,}/cipherbox-api" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      - name: Extract component versions
        id: versions
        run: |
          API_VERSION=$(node -e "console.log(require('./apps/api/package.json').version)")
          echo "api=${API_VERSION}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - uses: docker/login-action@650006c6eb7dba73a995cc03b0b2d7f5ca915bee # v4.2.0
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - uses: docker/build-push-action@f9f3042f7e2789586610d6e8b85c8f03e5195baf # v7.2.0
        with:
          context: .
          file: apps/api/Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: |
            ${{ env.API_IMAGE }}:${{ steps.versions.outputs.api }}
            ${{ env.API_IMAGE }}:latest-staging
            ${{ env.API_IMAGE }}:${{ env.DEPLOY_TAG }}

  build-tee:
    name: Build & Push TEE Worker Image
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
        with:
          ref: ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}

      - name: Set lowercase image name
        run: echo "TEE_IMAGE=ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER,,}/cipherbox-tee-worker" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      - name: Extract component versions
        id: versions
        run: |
          TEE_VERSION=$(node -e "console.log(require('./apps/tee-worker/package.json').version)")
          echo "tee=${TEE_VERSION}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - uses: docker/login-action@650006c6eb7dba73a995cc03b0b2d7f5ca915bee # v4.2.0
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - uses: docker/build-push-action@f9f3042f7e2789586610d6e8b85c8f03e5195baf # v7.2.0
        with:
          context: .
          file: apps/tee-worker/Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: |
            ${{ env.TEE_IMAGE }}:${{ steps.versions.outputs.tee }}
            ${{ env.TEE_IMAGE }}:latest-staging
            ${{ env.TEE_IMAGE }}:${{ env.DEPLOY_TAG }}

  build-web:
    name: Build Web App
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
        with:
          ref: ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}

      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@0ebf47130e4866e96fce0953f49152a61190b271 # v6.0.9

      - uses: actions/setup-node@48b55a011bda9f5d6aeb4c2d9c7362e8dae4041e # v6.4.0
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: 'pnpm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Build shared packages
        run: |
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/crypto build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/core build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/api-client build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/sdk-core build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/sdk build

      - name: Build web app with staging env vars
        run: pnpm --filter @cipherbox/web build
        env:
          VITE_WEB3AUTH_CLIENT_ID: ${{ vars.VITE_WEB3AUTH_CLIENT_ID }}
          VITE_API_URL: ${{ vars.STAGING_API_URL }}
          VITE_ENVIRONMENT: staging
          VITE_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID: ${{ vars.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID }}
          VITE_FARO_URL: ${{ vars.VITE_FARO_URL }}
          GRAFANA_FARO_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GRAFANA_FARO_API_KEY }}
          GRAFANA_STACK_ID: ${{ vars.GRAFANA_STACK_ID }}

      - name: Upload web dist as artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@043fb46d1a93c77aae656e7c1c64a875d1fc6a0a # v7.0.1
        with:
          name: web-dist
          path: apps/web/dist/
          retention-days: 1

  create-desktop-release:
    name: Create Desktop Release
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - name: Create or update GitHub Release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          TAG="${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}"
          BODY="Staging build for ${TAG}. macOS (unsigned - right-click > Open to launch), Windows (unsigned - click \"More info\" > \"Run anyway\"), and Linux (AppImage/deb)."
          # Create the release if it doesn't exist yet; ignore error if it does.
          # Not marked as prerelease — staging is the production environment and
          # /releases/latest/ must resolve to these builds for the Tauri auto-updater.
          gh release create "$TAG" \
            --repo "${{ github.repository }}" \
            --title "CipherBox Desktop ${TAG}" \
            --notes "$BODY" \
            2>/dev/null || true

  build-desktop:
    name: Build Desktop App (macOS)
    needs: [create-desktop-release]
    runs-on: macos-latest
    environment: staging
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
        with:
          ref: ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}

      - name: Install FUSE-T
        run: |
          brew install --cask fuse-t
          sudo mkdir -p /usr/local/lib/pkgconfig
          sudo ln -sf "/Library/Application Support/fuse-t/pkgconfig/fuse-t.pc" /usr/local/lib/pkgconfig/fuse.pc

      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@0ebf47130e4866e96fce0953f49152a61190b271 # v6.0.9

      - uses: actions/setup-node@48b55a011bda9f5d6aeb4c2d9c7362e8dae4041e # v6.4.0
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: 'pnpm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Build shared packages
        run: |
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/crypto build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/core build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/api-client build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/sdk-core build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/sdk build

      - uses: tauri-apps/tauri-action@84b9d35b5fc46c1e45415bdb6144030364f7ebc5 # v0.6.2
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD }}
          VITE_WEB3AUTH_CLIENT_ID: ${{ vars.VITE_WEB3AUTH_CLIENT_ID }}
          VITE_API_URL: ${{ vars.STAGING_API_URL }}
          VITE_ENVIRONMENT: staging
          VITE_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID: ${{ vars.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID }}
          VITE_FARO_URL: ${{ vars.VITE_FARO_URL }}
          GRAFANA_FARO_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GRAFANA_FARO_API_KEY }}
          GRAFANA_STACK_ID: ${{ vars.GRAFANA_STACK_ID }}
        with:
          projectPath: apps/desktop
          tauriScript: pnpm tauri
          tagName: ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}
          releaseName: 'CipherBox Desktop ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}'
          releaseBody: 'Staging build for ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}. macOS (unsigned - right-click > Open to launch) and Windows (unsigned - click "More info" > "Run anyway").'
          releaseDraft: false
          prerelease: false
          includeUpdaterJson: true

  build-desktop-windows:
    name: Build Desktop App (Windows)
    needs: [create-desktop-release]
    runs-on: windows-latest
    environment: staging
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
        with:
          ref: ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}

      - name: Install WinFsp
        shell: powershell
        run: |
          $url = "https://github.com/winfsp/winfsp/releases/download/v2.1/winfsp-2.1.25156.msi"
          # Use Join-Path to produce proper Windows backslash paths —
          # msiexec.exe treats '/' as a flag prefix, so forward slashes in
          # the file path cause "package could not be opened" errors.
          $resourceDir = Join-Path "${{ github.workspace }}" "apps\desktop\src-tauri\resources"
          $out = Join-Path $resourceDir "winfsp-2.1.25156.msi"
          $expectedHash = "073A70E00F77423E34BED98B86E600DEF93393BA5822204FAC57A29324DB9F7A"
          New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $resourceDir
          Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $url -OutFile $out
          $actualHash = (Get-FileHash $out -Algorithm SHA256).Hash
          if ($actualHash -ne $expectedHash) { throw "WinFsp MSI hash mismatch: expected $expectedHash, got $actualHash" }
          $proc = Start-Process msiexec.exe -ArgumentList "/i","`"$out`"","/qn","INSTALLLEVEL=1000" -Wait -NoNewWindow -PassThru
          if ($proc.ExitCode -ne 0) { throw "msiexec failed with exit code $($proc.ExitCode)" }
          # winfsp-sys build.rs reads HKLM\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\WinFsp\InstallDir
          # to find headers/libs. The MSI doesn't reliably write this key on CI runners.
          $installDir = "C:\Program Files (x86)\WinFsp"
          if (!(Test-Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\WinFsp")) {
            New-Item -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\WinFsp" -Force | Out-Null
          }
          New-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\WinFsp" -Name "InstallDir" -Value $installDir -PropertyType String -Force | Out-Null
          # Verify registry key was written correctly
          $regVal = Get-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\WinFsp" -Name "InstallDir" -ErrorAction Stop
          if (-not $regVal.InstallDir -or $regVal.InstallDir -ne $installDir) {
            throw "WinFsp InstallDir registry mismatch: expected '$installDir', got '$($regVal.InstallDir)'"
          }
          Write-Host "WinFsp InstallDir registry: $($regVal.InstallDir)"
          if (!(Test-Path "$installDir\lib")) { throw "WinFsp lib directory not found at $installDir\lib" }
          if (!(Test-Path "$installDir\inc")) { throw "WinFsp inc directory not found at $installDir\inc" }

      - name: Install Rust toolchain
        run: rustup default stable

      - uses: actions/cache@27d5ce7f107fe9357f9df03efb73ab90386fccae # v5.0.5
        with:
          path: |
            ~/.cargo/registry
            ~/.cargo/git
            apps/desktop/src-tauri/target
          key: windows-cargo-${{ hashFiles('apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.lock') }}
          restore-keys: windows-cargo-

      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@0ebf47130e4866e96fce0953f49152a61190b271 # v6.0.9

      - uses: actions/setup-node@48b55a011bda9f5d6aeb4c2d9c7362e8dae4041e # v6.4.0
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: 'pnpm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Build shared packages
        run: |
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/crypto build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/core build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/api-client build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/sdk-core build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/sdk build

      - uses: tauri-apps/tauri-action@84b9d35b5fc46c1e45415bdb6144030364f7ebc5 # v0.6.2
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD }}
          VITE_WEB3AUTH_CLIENT_ID: ${{ vars.VITE_WEB3AUTH_CLIENT_ID }}
          VITE_API_URL: ${{ vars.STAGING_API_URL }}
          VITE_ENVIRONMENT: staging
          VITE_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID: ${{ vars.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID }}
          VITE_FARO_URL: ${{ vars.VITE_FARO_URL }}
          GRAFANA_FARO_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GRAFANA_FARO_API_KEY }}
          GRAFANA_STACK_ID: ${{ vars.GRAFANA_STACK_ID }}
        with:
          projectPath: apps/desktop
          tauriScript: pnpm tauri
          tagName: ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}
          releaseName: 'CipherBox Desktop ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}'
          releaseBody: 'Staging build for ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}. macOS (unsigned - right-click > Open to launch), Windows (unsigned - click "More info" > "Run anyway"), and Linux (AppImage/deb).'
          releaseDraft: false
          prerelease: false
          includeUpdaterJson: true
          args: -- --no-default-features --features winfsp

  build-desktop-linux:
    name: Build Desktop App (Linux)
    needs: [create-desktop-release]
    runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
    environment: staging
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
        with:
          ref: ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}

      - name: Install system dependencies
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y \
            libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev \
            libayatana-appindicator3-dev \
            librsvg2-dev \
            libssl-dev \
            libxdo-dev \
            libfuse3-dev \
            pkg-config \
            build-essential

      - name: Install Rust toolchain
        run: rustup default stable

      - uses: actions/cache@27d5ce7f107fe9357f9df03efb73ab90386fccae # v5.0.5
        with:
          path: |
            ~/.cargo/registry
            ~/.cargo/git
            apps/desktop/src-tauri/target
          key: linux-cargo-${{ hashFiles('apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.lock') }}
          restore-keys: linux-cargo-

      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@0ebf47130e4866e96fce0953f49152a61190b271 # v6.0.9

      - uses: actions/setup-node@48b55a011bda9f5d6aeb4c2d9c7362e8dae4041e # v6.4.0
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: 'pnpm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Build shared packages
        run: |
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/crypto build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/core build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/api-client build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/sdk-core build
          pnpm --filter @cipherbox/sdk build

      - uses: tauri-apps/tauri-action@84b9d35b5fc46c1e45415bdb6144030364f7ebc5 # v0.6.2
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD }}
          VITE_WEB3AUTH_CLIENT_ID: ${{ vars.VITE_WEB3AUTH_CLIENT_ID }}
          VITE_API_URL: ${{ vars.STAGING_API_URL }}
          VITE_ENVIRONMENT: staging
          VITE_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID: ${{ vars.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID }}
          VITE_FARO_URL: ${{ vars.VITE_FARO_URL }}
          GRAFANA_FARO_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GRAFANA_FARO_API_KEY }}
          GRAFANA_STACK_ID: ${{ vars.GRAFANA_STACK_ID }}
        with:
          projectPath: apps/desktop
          tauriScript: pnpm tauri
          tagName: ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}
          releaseName: 'CipherBox Desktop ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}'
          releaseBody: 'Staging build for ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}. macOS (unsigned - right-click > Open to launch), Windows (unsigned - click "More info" > "Run anyway"), and Linux (AppImage/deb).'
          releaseDraft: false
          prerelease: false
          includeUpdaterJson: true
          args: -- --no-default-features --features fuse

  deploy-vps:
    name: Deploy to Staging VPS
    needs: [build-api, build-tee, build-web]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
        with:
          ref: ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}

      - name: Download web dist artifact
        uses: actions/download-artifact@3e5f45b2cfb9172054b4087a40e8e0b5a5461e7c # v8.0.1
        with:
          name: web-dist
          path: web-dist/

      - name: Generate .env.staging
        run: |
          cat > .env.staging << 'ENVEOF'
          NODE_ENV=staging
          CIPHERBOX_ENVIRONMENT=staging
          TEST_LOGIN_SECRET=${{ secrets.STAGING_TEST_LOGIN_SECRET }}
          PORT=3000
          DB_HOST=postgres
          DB_PORT=5432
          DB_USERNAME=${{ vars.STAGING_DB_USERNAME }}
          DB_PASSWORD=REDACTED secrets.STAGING_DB_PASSWORD }}
          DB_DATABASE=cipherbox_staging
          JWT_SECRET=${{ secrets.STAGING_JWT_SECRET }}
          CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS=${{ vars.CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS }}
          IPFS_PROVIDER=local
          IPFS_LOCAL_API_URL=http://ipfs:5001
          IPFS_LOCAL_GATEWAY_URL=http://ipfs:8080
          DELEGATED_ROUTING_URL=http://someguy:8190
          DELEGATED_ROUTING_FALLBACK_URL=https://delegated-ipfs.dev
          THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET=${{ secrets.STAGING_THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET }}
          REDIS_HOST=redis
          REDIS_PORT=6379
          TEE_WORKER_URL=http://tee-worker:3001
          TEE_WORKER_SECRET=${{ secrets.STAGING_TEE_WORKER_SECRET }}
          REDIS_PASSWORD=REDACTED secrets.STAGING_REDIS_PASSWORD }}
          GRAFANA_LOKI_URL=${{ vars.GRAFANA_LOKI_URL }}
          GRAFANA_LOKI_USERNAME=${{ vars.GRAFANA_LOKI_USERNAME }}
          GRAFANA_LOKI_API_KEY=${{ secrets.GRAFANA_LOKI_API_KEY }}
          GRAFANA_PROMETHEUS_URL=${{ vars.GRAFANA_PROMETHEUS_URL }}
          GRAFANA_PROMETHEUS_USERNAME=${{ vars.GRAFANA_PROMETHEUS_USERNAME }}
          GRAFANA_PROMETHEUS_API_KEY=${{ secrets.GRAFANA_PROMETHEUS_API_KEY }}
          SENDGRID_API_KEY=${{ secrets.SENDGRID_API_KEY }}
          SENDGRID_FROM_EMAIL=${{ vars.SENDGRID_FROM_EMAIL }}
          GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=${{ vars.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID }}
          IDENTITY_JWT_PRIVATE_KEY=${{ secrets.IDENTITY_JWT_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          ENVEOF
          # Append image tag, lowercase owner, and component versions (can't use shell vars in quoted heredoc)
          OWNER="${{ github.repository_owner }}"
          echo "GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER=${OWNER,,}" >> .env.staging
          echo "TAG=${{ env.DEPLOY_TAG }}" >> .env.staging
          API_VER=$(node -e "console.log(require('./apps/api/package.json').version)")
          TEE_VER=$(node -e "console.log(require('./apps/tee-worker/package.json').version)")
          echo "API_VERSION=${API_VER}" >> .env.staging
          echo "TEE_VERSION=${TEE_VER}" >> .env.staging

      - name: Copy files to VPS
        uses: appleboy/scp-action@ff85246acaad7bdce478db94a363cd2bf7c90345 # v1.0.0
        with:
          host: ${{ vars.STAGING_HOST }}
          username: ${{ vars.STAGING_USER }}
          key: ${{ secrets.STAGING_SSH_KEY }}
          source: '.env.staging,docker/docker-compose.staging.yml,docker/Caddyfile,docker/alloy-config.river'
          target: /opt/cipherbox
          strip_components: 0

      - name: Arrange files on VPS
        uses: appleboy/ssh-action@0ff4204d59e8e51228ff73bce53f80d53301dee2 # v1.2.5
        with:
          host: ${{ vars.STAGING_HOST }}
          username: ${{ vars.STAGING_USER }}
          key: ${{ secrets.STAGING_SSH_KEY }}
          script: |
            # Move files to correct locations
            mv /opt/cipherbox/.env.staging /opt/cipherbox/docker/.env.staging 2>/dev/null || true
            cd /opt/cipherbox/docker

            # Docker Compose reads .env automatically for variable substitution
            cp .env.staging .env

            # Restrict env file permissions (contains secrets)
            chmod 600 .env .env.staging

            # Ensure certs symlink exists for Caddy
            rm -rf /opt/cipherbox/docker/certs
            ln -sf /opt/cipherbox/certs /opt/cipherbox/docker/certs

      - name: Deploy web app files to VPS
        uses: appleboy/scp-action@ff85246acaad7bdce478db94a363cd2bf7c90345 # v1.0.0
        with:
          host: ${{ vars.STAGING_HOST }}
          username: ${{ vars.STAGING_USER }}
          key: ${{ secrets.STAGING_SSH_KEY }}
          source: 'web-dist/*'
          target: /opt/cipherbox/web
          strip_components: 1
          rm: true

      - name: Deploy services
        uses: appleboy/ssh-action@0ff4204d59e8e51228ff73bce53f80d53301dee2 # v1.2.5
        with:
          host: ${{ vars.STAGING_HOST }}
          username: ${{ vars.STAGING_USER }}
          key: ${{ secrets.STAGING_SSH_KEY }}
          script: |
            set -euo pipefail
            cd /opt/cipherbox/docker

            # Login to GHCR
            echo "${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}" | docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ github.actor }} --password-stdin

            # Set image tag from git tag (GHCR requires lowercase owner)
            export TAG="${{ env.DEPLOY_TAG }}"
            OWNER="${{ github.repository_owner }}"
            export GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER="${OWNER,,}"

            # Pull new images
            docker compose -f docker-compose.staging.yml pull

            # Run database migrations before starting services
            # (api service inherits env vars from env_file in compose)
            docker compose -f docker-compose.staging.yml run --rm \
              api node dist/run-migrations.js

            # Start/restart services
            docker compose -f docker-compose.staging.yml up -d

            # Restart Caddy to pick up refreshed web files bind mount
            # (scp rm:true recreates the host dir, breaking the old mount inode)
            docker compose -f docker-compose.staging.yml restart caddy

            # Cleanup old images
            docker image prune -f

  provision-dashboard:
    name: Provision Grafana Dashboard
    needs: [deploy-vps]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
        with:
          ref: ${{ inputs.staging_tag || github.ref_name }}

      - name: Wait for Grafana Cloud readiness
        env:
          GRAFANA_URL: ${{ vars.GRAFANA_URL }}
          GRAFANA_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GRAFANA_API_KEY }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          : "${GRAFANA_URL:?GRAFANA_URL is required for Grafana readiness check}"
          : "${GRAFANA_API_KEY:?GRAFANA_API_KEY is required for Grafana readiness check}"
          GRAFANA_URL="${GRAFANA_URL%/}"
          MAX_ATTEMPTS=30
          INTERVAL=10
          for ((i=1; i<=MAX_ATTEMPTS; i++)); do
            HTTP_CODE=$(curl -sS --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 15 \
              -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" \
              -H "Authorization: Bearer ${GRAFANA_API_KEY}" \
              "${GRAFANA_URL}/api/health") || HTTP_CODE=000
            if [[ "$HTTP_CODE" == "200" ]]; then
              echo "Grafana Cloud is ready (attempt $i/$MAX_ATTEMPTS)"
              exit 0
            elif [[ "$HTTP_CODE" =~ ^(401|403|404)$ ]]; then
              echo "::error::Grafana returned HTTP $HTTP_CODE — check GRAFANA_URL and GRAFANA_API_KEY"
              exit 1
            fi
            echo "Grafana not ready (HTTP $HTTP_CODE), waiting ${INTERVAL}s... ($i/$MAX_ATTEMPTS)"
            sleep "$INTERVAL"
          done
          echo "::error::Grafana Cloud did not become ready after $((MAX_ATTEMPTS * INTERVAL))s"
          exit 1

      - name: Push dashboard to Grafana Cloud
        env:
          GRAFANA_URL: ${{ vars.GRAFANA_URL }}
          GRAFANA_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GRAFANA_API_KEY }}
          DS_METRICS_UID: ${{ vars.GRAFANA_DS_METRICS_UID }}
          DS_LOGS_UID: ${{ vars.GRAFANA_DS_LOGS_UID }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          : "${GRAFANA_URL:?GRAFANA_URL is required}"
          : "${GRAFANA_API_KEY:?GRAFANA_API_KEY is required}"
          : "${DS_METRICS_UID:?GRAFANA_DS_METRICS_UID is required}"
          : "${DS_LOGS_UID:?GRAFANA_DS_LOGS_UID is required}"
          GRAFANA_URL="${GRAFANA_URL%/}"

          # The dashboard JSON uses __inputs for datasource templating.
          # Replace variable references with actual datasource UIDs.
          DASHBOARD=$(cat docker/grafana/dashboards/cipherbox-staging.json \
            | jq --arg metrics "$DS_METRICS_UID" --arg logs "$DS_LOGS_UID" \
                 'del(.__inputs)
                  | .id = null
                  | walk(if type == "object" and .uid? and (.uid | test("\\$\\{DS_")) then
                      .uid = (if .uid == "${DS_GRAFANA_CLOUD_METRICS}" then $metrics
                              elif .uid == "${DS_GRAFANA_CLOUD_LOGS}" then $logs
                              else .uid end)
                    else . end)')

          # Fail if any datasource placeholder survived the rewrite
          if jq -e '.. | objects | .uid? | select(type == "string" and test("^\\$\\{DS_"))' \
            >/dev/null <<<"$DASHBOARD"; then
            echo "::error::Unresolved datasource placeholder(s) remain in dashboard JSON"
            exit 1
          fi

          # Wrap in import payload
          PAYLOAD=$(jq -n --argjson dashboard "$DASHBOARD" '{
            dashboard: $dashboard,
            overwrite: true,
            message: "Provisioned by deploy-staging workflow"
          }')

          # Push to Grafana API
          HTTP_CODE=$(curl -sS --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 60 \
            -o /tmp/grafana-response.json -w "%{http_code}" \
            -X POST "${GRAFANA_URL}/api/dashboards/db" \
            -H "Authorization: Bearer ${GRAFANA_API_KEY}" \
            -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
            -d "$PAYLOAD")

          if [[ ! "$HTTP_CODE" =~ ^2[0-9][0-9]$ ]]; then
            echo "::error::Grafana API returned HTTP $HTTP_CODE"
            cat /tmp/grafana-response.json
            exit 1
          fi

          echo "Dashboard provisioned successfully (HTTP $HTTP_CODE)"
          jq -r '.url // "unknown"' /tmp/grafana-response.json

name: cipherbox-staging

x-logging: &default-logging
  driver: json-file
  options:
    max-size: '10m'
    max-file: '3'

services:
  api:
    image: ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER:-OWNER}/cipherbox-api:${TAG:-latest}
    restart: unless-stopped
    env_file: .env.staging
    ports:
      - '127.0.0.1:3000:3000'
    logging: *default-logging
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy

  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USERNAME:-cipherbox}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_DATABASE:-cipherbox_staging}
    ports:
      - '127.0.0.1:5432:5432'
    volumes:

content.text:
The compose file is revealing — two infra-level suspects jump out, and one of them is more likely than my datastore hypothesis:

1. **The `ipfs` (Kubo) container is CPU-capped at `1.0` core** (and someguy at another `1.0`), on a 4-vCPU box (lines 84-88). Kubo is the upload/IPNS bottleneck — pinning it to a single core would directly halve throughput under concurrency.
2. **`IPFS_PROFILE: server,pebbleds` is declared, but the comment (lines 66-68) warns it only applies to a *fresh* repo** — if the `ipfs_staging` volume wasn't wiped, the on-disk datastore could still be flatfs regardless of this env.

Both are config, not code. Let me check git history for when these were introduced (relative to the March 19.2 baseline) and verify the 1Password SSH agent before connecting.

The git history **refutes both of my infra hypotheses** — important to be precise here:

- **Kubo's 1-CPU cap is not new.** `cpus: '1.0'` traces to `0e9cb1e0e` (2026-03-23), *before* the 19.2 pebbleds baseline (`8f8f03fa6`, 03-24). The good baseline was captured *with* Kubo already pinned to one core — so the cap is a real bottleneck but it's a constant, not the regression.
- **pebbleds is still declared and unchanged** since 03-24; the only staging-compose change since is the May TEE-worker swap (#472), which doesn't touch the upload path.

So the infra config hasn't meaningfully changed since the good baseline — which points the finger at **deployed API/SDK code or accumulated data/state**, not compose config. The decisive test is the server-side Prometheus histograms: if Kubo pin/publish latency doubled, it's infra/data-bloat; if it's flat, the regression is client/SDK-side.

content.text:
Root cause confirmed — and it's **operational data bloat, not a code regression.**

## The evidence chain

| Signal | 19.2 baseline | Now | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Kubo `pin` mean (server-side)** | 1.37s | **3.02s** | **+120%** |
| POST `/ipfs/upload` mean | — | 3.22s | of which **3.02s is the Kubo pin** → API overhead ~0.2s |
| IPFS repo size | ~320 MiB | **6.2 GB** | 294,811 objects |
| Actually pinned / live | — | **17,875 CIDs / ~489 MB** | `pinned_cids` table agrees (17,867 rows) |

The upload endpoint spends **3.0 of its 3.2 seconds inside the Kubo pin call** — so the regression is squarely in Kubo, not API/SDK code (the API jumped 0.24→0.43 but adds only ~0.2s of overhead). And the smoking gun: **the repo is 6.2 GB / 294k objects, but only ~489 MB / 17,875 CIDs are pinned/live — ~90% of the datastore is unpinned garbage** from three months of load-test churn (create→delete leaves orphaned blocks until GC). That 6.2 GB pebbleds store vastly exceeds Kubo's 2 GB memory cap (currently 71% used), so pins hit disk on the write path → latency doubles → throughput halves.

Everything else is unchanged from the good baseline, which is why it *isn't* the cause: **2 vCPU** (134-day uptime spans the March baseline), **Kubo CPU cap 1.0** (since 03-23), **datastore confirmed `pebbleds`** (type/format v24 on disk), **Kubo v0.40.0**. The compose config and box are constants; only accumulated state changed.

## The fix (cheap, low-risk, high-confidence)

1. **`ipfs repo gc`** on staging — reclaims the ~5.7 GB of unpinned garbage. GC only removes *unpinned* blocks, so live files are untouched. Expect repo 6.2 GB → ~0.5–1 GB.
2. **Re-run `upload-throughput`** @ 50/100/200 — I expect pin to drop back toward ~1.4s and throughput toward ~15/18/19 ops/s. That both confirms the diagnosis and tells you whether *any* residual regression is real code.
3. **Longer-term:** enable Kubo's periodic GC (daemon `--enable-gc` / `Datastore.GCPeriod`) or a cron so this can't silently recur; consider bumping Kubo's mem cap (2 G → 3–4 G — there's headroom, host is at 2.8/7.8 GiB). Also a methodology note: **the load test itself generates this garbage**, so future baseline runs should GC first, or the harness should clean up its test accounts' content (it deletes accounts but the blocks linger until GC).

## Want me to proceed?

This is where I stop and check — running GC mutates your staging instance, and you're mid-deployment. My recommendation:

- **(a) Run `ipfs repo gc` now + re-run `upload-throughput` @ 50/100/200** to confirm recovery — ~20 min, gives you a clean before/after. *(recommended)*
- **(b) Just GC, no re-run** — fastest path to restore staging perf.
- **(c) Hold** — I've given you the diagnosis; you handle the GC on your own schedule.

I'd also still like to **(d) persist these 7 runs as fresh `tests/load/baselines/` + a dated `.planning/baselines/` doc** regardless — but I'd run that *after* a post-GC re-measure so the recorded baseline reflects a clean datastore, not the bloated one. Which do you want?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Sequential staging load-test sweep.
# Dispatches load-test.yml runs one at a time (never concurrent -> respects the
# "no concurrent staging load tests" rule), polls each to completion, and
# downloads its metrics artifact. NOT committed; scratch tooling for a one-off sweep.
set -uo pipefail

REPO="FSM1/cipher-box"
WF_FILE="load-test.yml"
WF_ID="249928808"
OUTDIR="${1:?usage: staging-loadtest-sweep.sh <outdir>}"
LOG="$OUTDIR/progress.log"
SUMMARY="$OUTDIR/summary.tsv"
mkdir -p "$OUTDIR"

log() { echo "[$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)] $*" | tee -a "$LOG"; }
gh_retry() { local i; for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh "$@" 2>>"$LOG" && return 0; sleep 5; done; return 1; }

runs=(
  "mixed-workload:50"
  "mixed-workload:100"
  "mixed-workload:200"
  "sustained-load:200"
  "upload-throughput:50"
  "upload-throughput:100"
  "upload-throughput:200"
)

printf 'scenario\tclients\trun_id\tconclusion\tartifact_dir\n' > "$SUMMARY"
log "=== Staging load-test sweep: ${#runs[@]} runs against $REPO ==="

for spec in "${runs[@]}"; do
  scenario="${spec%%:*}"; clients="${spec##*:}"
  label="$scenario @ ${clients} clients"
  log "--- Dispatching: $label ---"

  before="$(gh_retry api "repos/$REPO/actions/workflows/$WF_ID/runs?per_page=1" --jq '.workflow_runs[0].id' || echo 0)"

  if ! gh_retry workflow run "$WF_FILE" -f environment=staging -f scenario="$scenario" -f client_count="$clients"; then
    log "!! DISPATCH FAILED for $label -- skipping"
    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$scenario" "$clients" "-" "dispatch_failed" "-" >> "$SUMMARY"
    continue
  fi

  runid=""
  for _ in $(seq 1 36); do
    sleep 5
    latest="$(gh_retry api "repos/$REPO/actions/workflows/$WF_ID/runs?per_page=1" --jq '.workflow_runs[0].id' || echo 0)"
    if [ "$latest" != "$before" ] && [ "$latest" != "0" ]; then runid="$latest"; break; fi
  done
  if [ -z "$runid" ]; then
    log "!! Could not capture run id for $label -- skipping"
    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$scenario" "$clients" "-" "no_run_id" "-" >> "$SUMMARY"
    continue
  fi
  log "Run id $runid ($label) -> https://github.com/$REPO/actions/runs/$runid"

  status="queued"
  while [ "$status" != "completed" ]; do
    sleep 20
    status="$(gh_retry api "repos/$REPO/actions/runs/$runid" --jq '.status' || echo unknown)"
  done
  concl="$(gh_retry api "repos/$REPO/actions/runs/$runid" --jq '.conclusion' || echo unknown)"
  log "Run $runid completed: conclusion=$concl"

  rundir="$OUTDIR/${scenario}-${clients}c"
  mkdir -p "$rundir"
  if gh_retry run download "$runid" -R "$REPO" -D "$rundir"; then
    log "Artifacts -> $rundir"
  else
    log "No artifact downloaded for $label (conclusion=$concl)"
  fi
  printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$scenario" "$clients" "$runid" "$concl" "$rundir" >> "$SUMMARY"
done

log "=== SWEEP COMPLETE ==="

content.text: The grep surfaced a critical detail at line 123 — it's a **Counter, not a Gauge**. That changes the answer. Let me read the actual drift logic to be precise.

Pulled the actual logic (`pending-unpin.processor.ts:93` `runDriftReport()`) — and there are two corrections to make, one of which matters a lot.

**1. The value is 39, not 32.**

**2. It's a cumulative `Counter`, not a gauge — so 39 is *not* "items currently orphaned."** The code (`metrics.service.ts:184` `new client.Counter`) `.inc()`s once per orphaned CID *on every hourly drift run* and never resets (except on container restart). The comment at line 123 spells this out: it's an append-only count of orphan *detections* over time, for trend/alerting. Since the API container was only ~2h old at capture, 39 = the orphans summed across however many hourly runs fired in that window — the same persistently-orphaned CID gets re-counted each run. To read it as a live count you'd have to divide by the number of runs, which you can't do from the counter alone.

**3. The definition is slightly broader than you said.** An "orphan" is a **recursive** Kubo pin whose CID is in **neither `pinned_cids` *nor* `pending_unpins`**:

```
orphan = (cid ∈ kubo `pin ls --type=recursive`)  AND  (cid ∉ pinned_cids ∪ pending_unpins)
```

So it excludes pending_unpins (CIDs already queued for removal aren't flagged), and only looks at recursive pins (indirect/child pins are ignored). Raw-string CID compare — same as my set-diff below would be.

**What the *actual current* count looks like:** from the pre-GC snapshot — Kubo recursive pins **17,875**, `pinned_cids` **17,867**, `pending_unpins` **0** — the net gap is only **8** (orphaned − missing = 8). So the true live drift is single/low-double digits, well under 0.05% of pins — not hundreds. GC doesn't touch pinned blocks, so that's still ~current.

If you want the exact distinct orphan count (`|kubo_recursive \ (pinned_cids ∪ pending_unpins)|`) plus the reverse "missing" set, I can compute it directly with a set-diff on staging — but I'd run it **after the recheck finishes**, since the recheck is actively creating/deleting pins right now and would pollute the snapshot with transient mid-flight discrepancies. And the counter reading `39` happens to equal the live count because the hourly drift job has run exactly once since the 2h-old container started. The 39 orphaned are a minor block leak; the 31 missing are DB rows whose files Kubo can't serve.

## Recheck verdict: GC did **not** restore throughput — my bloat hypothesis is largely refuted

Server-side pin latency, isolated to just the recheck's 21,184 pins:

| | 19.2 baseline | pre-GC sweep | **post-GC recheck** |
|---|---|---|---|

The repo is now **69k objects / 3.2 GB** (was 294k / 6.2 GB) — ~4× fewer objects — yet pin latency is **no better** (arguably worse). The recheck is **confounded**: it ran (a) immediately after GC while pebbleds was still compacting 274k deletions, and (b) after ~2 hours of continuous heavy load from my sweeps. 2. **API/SDK code** (0.24→0.43) adding upload-path work.

content.text:
Possibly — but with caveats, and it's easy to fool yourself with it.

**What a Kubo restart actually does:** clears all in-memory state — goroutines, the connection manager, the DHT routing table, the **reprovider queue**, and accumulated heap pressure (Kubo was at 1.55/2 GiB = 77% of its cap after 2h of load). It re-opens pebbleds with a **cold block cache**. No data loss — the volume persists, all 17,875 pins survive. Cost: ~30s where the API can't pin/upload.

**Why it might help:** if the regression is partly *transient runtime degradation* — heap near the cap forcing aggressive Go GC, a backed-up reprovider, connection churn, or pebbleds state right after the GC's 274k-delete compaction — a fresh daemon relieves all of that. Given I hammered staging for ~2h straight, some of the slowdown is plausibly this.

**Why it's a measurement trap:** a fresh daemon starts with an **empty reprovide queue and cold caches**, so you get a **honeymoon window** — fast pins for a few minutes, then it decays as the reprovider re-engages (reproviding 17,875 pins to the DHT via someguy is real work on the 1-CPU cap) and load resumes. So *restart → immediately re-test → "it's fixed!"* would be a false positive. And it won't touch a **structural** cause (pinset size, the 1-CPU cap, or API/SDK code).

**To use it as a real signal, the sequence matters:**
1. Restart Kubo
2. Let it idle ~10–15 min (reprovider scheduled, caches warm, post-GC compaction advances)
3. One clean `upload-throughput@50`

If perf returns to ~baseline **and holds** → the cause was transient runtime state, and periodic restart (or reprovider tuning) is a legit mitigation. If it spikes good then **decays** → structural (pinset/CPU/code), and restart only buys minutes.

On GC: it's already run today (#547 tracks automating it), and the recheck showed GC alone didn't restore throughput — so treat GC as hygiene, not the perf fix.

Want me to run that restart-then-settle-then-retest sequence? It's a ~30s staging blip plus a ~15 min idle — your call on timing since you're mid-deploy. I won't touch it until you say go.

Good question — and it's worth checking properly rather than reasoning alone. someguy is the delegated-routing sidecar (accelerated DHT), co-located with Kubo on the 2-vCPU box (each capped at 1 CPU). The crux is: **is it on the *synchronous* upload/pin path, or only the IPNS publish/resolve path — and is it healthy or falling back?**

Per ultracode I'll fan out a code-path map in parallel while I pull the decisive live evidence from staging (delegated-routing fallback rate, Kubo routing config, someguy health/load).

content.text:
Strong live evidence is in, and the answer is **no — someguy is not the primary cause** (it can't explain the halved throughput). Here's why:

**Kubo doesn't even use someguy.** `ipfs config Routing` returns `{"DelegatedRouters": ["auto"]}` — Kubo does its own content routing via the public auto routers, *not* the local sidecar. someguy is used only by the **API's IPNS publish/resolve** layer (via `DELEGATED_ROUTING_URL`). So the dominant upload cost — the Kubo **pin** (4.19s, a local blockstore + pinset op) — never touches someguy.

**someguy is mostly healthy, not a bottleneck.** Delegated-routing counters (cumulative over today's load):

| op | primary (someguy) success | fell back to public | fallback rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| publish | 70,161 | 1,839 | **~2.6%** |
| resolve | 4,683 | 187 | **~3.8%** |

97%+ of publishes and 96%+ of resolves succeed on the local someguy primary; only a small fraction hit the slow public `delegated-ipfs.dev`. someguy is idle now (CPU 1.4%, mem 667 MiB/2 GiB — comfortable). Its logs are *noisy* (25k lines/3h: libp2p identify failures, "cannot reserve inbound connection: resource limit exceeded", DNS misses) but that's normal accelerated-DHT churn, not failure.

**Where someguy *does* cost you (secondary):** it's on the IPNS publish path (publish mean 1.42s, up from 0.83s), and the ~2.6–3.8% fallbacks add public-internet round-trips to those ops. But in the SDK's upload pipeline the IPNS publishes run *concurrently* with — and are mostly masked behind — the two ~4.4s pins (ciphertext + folder metadata). Even if someguy publish were instant, upload latency would drop maybe ~15–20%, not 2×. So it's worth tuning for IPNS *tail* latency, but it's not the regression.

**The regression is still pin-bound:** Kubo pin 1.37s → 4.19s, a local op gated by the 1-CPU cap + the grown pinset/datastore state — independent of someguy.

I have the someguy-role code-map workflow running in parallel to confirm the one thing I'm asserting from config+architecture rather than a direct code read: that the server-side `pin` operation isn't synchronously blocking on any routing/provide call. I'll fold that in when it lands — but the live evidence already rules someguy out as the main driver.

content.text:
Workflow confirms it — and tightens the conclusion further (with a correction to my own preliminary estimate).

## someguy is definitively ruled out as the regression cause

The code-path map confirms:

1. **Not on the pin path.** The `pin` timer wraps exactly one call — `ipfsProvider.pinFile()` → `POST {kubo}/api/v0/add?pin=true` against the local Kubo node (`local.provider.ts:49`). No delegated-routing call, no synchronous DHT-provide. Kubo has no `Routing.Type` override, so announcing the CID happens in Kubo's **background** reprovider after `add` returns. The 4.19s pin latency is pure local Kubo add+pin.

2. **Correcting my earlier estimate:** I said someguy might cost ~15–20% via IPNS publish. That's wrong — **IPNS publish to someguy is fire-and-forget** (`ipns.service.ts`: DB upsert first, then `delegatedRouting.publish()` as a *detached* promise; the response never waits for DHT propagation). So someguy contributes **~0** to upload latency, not 15–20%.

3. The **only** place someguy is synchronously awaited is `GET /ipns/resolve` — a read path, and even there it's DB-cache-backed (falls through to the Postgres cache on `BAD_GATEWAY`). Not the upload bottleneck.

So the 2.6%/3.8% fallback rates and the noisy someguy logs are a **separate, background IPNS-propagation concern** (worth tracking for discoverability), but they have nothing to do with the halved upload throughput.

## Where that leaves the diagnosis

The regression is now isolated with high confidence to **Kubo's local pin operation: 1.37s → 4.19s**, gated by the 1-CPU cap and the grown pinset/pebbleds state. Everything else (someguy, datastore block-garbage, compose config, box CPU) is ruled out.

**The one decisive test left** to split the two remaining sub-causes — pure 1-CPU concurrency-queuing vs. higher per-pin cost from the 17,875-pin pinset:

- Let staging idle ~15–30 min (reprovide/compaction settle), then **`time ipfs add` a single small file at idle** (no concurrency).
  - ~tens of ms → the 4s is **concurrency queuing on 1 CPU** → fix is raising Kubo's CPU cap.

content.text: `vaults.is_byo_user` is the flag, joined via `pinned_cids.user_id = vaults.owner_id`. BYO users pin on their *own* node (CipherBox keeps an advisory row but doesn't pin on Kubo), so missing-from-Kubo is expected for them — the concerning ones are non-BYO. Pulling the missing CIDs with timestamps, BYO-status, and a local-block-presence check (read-only, offline — won't disturb the settle):

input.command:
export SSH_AUTH_SOCK="$HOME/Library/Group Containers/2BUA8C4S2C.com.1password/t/agent.sock"
ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new -o ConnectTimeout=15 root@76.13.151.200 'bash -s' <<'REMOTE'
set +e
export LC_ALL=C
cd /opt/cipherbox/docker || exit 1
CF=docker-compose.staging.yml
docker compose -f $CF exec -T ipfs ipfs pin ls --type=recursive --quiet </dev/null 2>/dev/null | LC_ALL=C sort -u > /tmp/kp.txt
docker compose -f $CF exec -T postgres sh -lc 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -tA -F"|" -c "select p.cid, p.pinned_at, p.size_bytes, p.user_id, coalesce(v.is_byo_user,false) from pinned_cids p left join vaults v on v.owner_id=p.user_id order by p.cid"' </dev/null 2>/dev/null | LC_ALL=C sort -t'|' -k1,1 > /tmp/pc.tsv
join -t'|' -1 1 -2 1 -v1 /tmp/pc.tsv /tmp/kp.txt > /tmp/missing.tsv
echo "kubo recursive pins=$(wc -l </tmp/kp.txt)  pinned_cids=$(wc -l </tmp/pc.tsv)  MISSING=$(wc -l </tmp/missing.tsv)"
echo "  BYO missing (expected, external-pinned): $(awk -F'|' '$5=="t"' /tmp/missing.tsv | wc -l)"
echo "  non-BYO missing (CONCERNING):            $(awk -F'|' '$5=="f"' /tmp/missing.tsv | wc -l)"
echo "  total bytes of missing: $(awk -F'|' '{s+=$3} END{printf "%d (%.1f MB)\n", s, s/1048576}' /tmp/missing.tsv)"
echo; echo "=== MISSING grouped by pinned_at date | byo(t/f) | count | bytes ==="
awk -F'|' '{d=$2; sub(/ .*/,"",d); print d"|"$5}' /tmp/missing.tsv | LC_ALL=C sort | uniq -c
echo; echo "=== pinned_at min / max of missing ==="; cut -d'|' -f2 /tmp/missing.tsv | LC_ALL=C sort | sed -n '1p;$p'
echo; echo "=== full missing rows:  pinned_at | size | byo | cid ==="
awk -F'|' '{printf "%s | %8s | %s | %s\n",$2,$3,$5,$1}' /tmp/missing.tsv | LC_ALL=C sort
echo; echo "=== non-BYO missing: is the block still on Kubo locally? (offline stat) ==="
awk -F'|' '$5=="f"{print $1}' /tmp/missing.tsv | head -15 | while read c; do
  out=$(timeout 8 docker compose -f $CF exec -T ipfs ipfs block stat --offline "$c" </dev/null 2>&1 | tr '\n' ' ')
  echo "$c -> $out"
done
echo DONE
REMOTE

Done — and the result is cleaner (and more concerning) than the BYO theory predicted. **All 31 are non-BYO**, so none are the benign "pinned on the user's own node" case.

## When they were added

All between **2026-03-28 and 2026-05-26** — none recent (latest is ~4 weeks ago):

| date | count |
|---|---|
| 2026-03-28 | 10 |
| 2026-03-29 | 1 |
| 2026-03-30 | 1 |
| 2026-04-01 | 1 |
| 2026-04-02 | 10 |

| 2026-04-14 | 1 |
| 2026-05-26 | 2 |

So this is **not** from today's deploy or load tests — it's accumulated historical drift. The two clusters (Mar 28, Apr 2) look like specific testing/dev sessions.

## What they are

- **All non-BYO** (`is_byo_user = f`) → they genuinely *should* be pinned on CipherBox's Kubo.
- **All tiny**: 16 B – 36 KB, **0.1 MB total**. All `bafkrei…` = CIDv1 **raw** single-block objects (small encrypted content/metadata blobs).
- **Genuinely gone, not just unpinned**: offline `block stat` on a 15-CID sample → *every one* "block was not found locally." Kubo has neither the pin nor the block.

## Likely mechanism (and an honest note about my GC)

These are **stale `pinned_cids` rows**: at some point the Kubo pin was lost (a failed/partial unpin that removed the pin but left the DB row, or a repo hiccup) **without** deleting the DB row. The blocks then lingered as *unpinned garbage* until a GC swept them. They were already unpinned before today — so my `ipfs repo gc` didn't *cause* the drift, but for any of these whose garbage block was still present this morning, **the GC cleared the last local copy.** The root cause is a DB↔Kubo reconciliation gap that predates today (the timestamps prove it).

## Why this matters for #547

This is the inverse of the orphan drift, and it has a sharper edge: **the system has no auto-repair for the "missing" direction** (the drift report is read-only). If these map to *real* user files, those files are now unfetchable (private encrypted blocks, almost certainly only ever stored on this Kubo). And it's a direct caution for the periodic-GC plan — **aggressive auto-GC must be paired with a reconcile step** (re-pin or prune stale rows), or GC will keep finalizing exactly this kind of loss.

The severity hinges on one thing I haven't checked yet: **are these 31 owned by real users or leftover test accounts?** (Test accounts CASCADE-delete their `pinned_cids` on deletion, so these surviving rows suggest real users — worth confirming.) Want me to pull the owner emails + file references for these 31 and check whether the content is still re-fetchable from the public DHT? That tells us if it's real data loss or just stale bookkeeping. (Settle timer's still running, so now's a good time.)

## ⚠️ Prerequisite: reconcile DB↔Kubo pin drift *before* enabling aggressive periodic GC

During the 2026-06-22 investigation we found **31 `pinned_cids` rows whose content Kubo no longer has pinned** — and the blocks are gone locally too (confirmed via offline `block stat`). These are stale DB rows where the Kubo recursive pin was lost without the row being cleaned up (pinned_at spans 2026-03-28 → 2026-05-26; ~0.1 MB total; all 3 owners are dev/owner test accounts, so no third-party loss in this instance).

**Why this blocks naive auto-GC:** aggressive periodic GC deletes any *unpinned* block. If a `pinned_cids` row has lost its Kubo recursive pin (drift), GC deletes the last local copy and turns recoverable drift into permanent loss. The existing `drift-report` job is read-only and only counts the **orphan** direction (Kubo-pinned but not in DB) — there is **no detection or auto-repair for the "missing" direction** (in DB but not pinned on Kubo).

**Required before/with enabling auto-GC:**

1. A reconciliation pass that, for every `pinned_cids` row, verifies a matching Kubo recursive pin and either (a) re-pins the content if still retrievable, or (b) prunes the stale row and refunds quota if the content is genuinely gone.
2. Run reconciliation **before** the first aggressive GC, then on a schedule alongside GC.
3. Extend `drift-report` to also detect/report (and optionally repair) the "missing" direction, not just orphans.

Without step 1, turning on `--enable-gc` / a GC cron would keep finalizing exactly this kind of loss.
EOF
)
for i in 1 2 3 4; do env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh issue comment 547 -R FSM1/cipher-box -b "$BODY" 2>&1 && break; sleep 4; done

content.text:
That's the answer — **your hypothesis is confirmed, with a specific mechanism.** `ipfs stats reprovide` is the smoking gun:

- **CIDs scheduled for providing: 76,300** (the ~17.9k pin roots + their DAG children) — vs "a couple hundred" at the 19.2 baseline. ~100–400× growth.
- Provider worker pool **near-saturated**: 14/16 active, burst workers maxed (1 queued), 2.6k in the provide queue.
- That background DHT-announcing consumes **~30–70% of Kubo's single core *at idle*** (CPU samples 54% / 73% / 27%, with no load test running).

So it's exactly as you suspected — **not** per-pin cost (idle pin is still ~tens of ms), but the **provider/reprovider system scaling with object count**. On a 1.0-CPU cap, half the core is now eaten by announcing 76k CIDs to the DHT, leaving far less to serve concurrent pin requests → queuing → multi-second pins under load.

## Final test closes the loop

post-restart `upload@50` (fresh daemon, 3G cap, settled): **9.1 ops/s, p50 5,571 ms, 0 errors.** The full ladder:

| run | throughput @50 | p50 |
|---|---|---|
| 19.2 baseline (Mar) | **15.10/s** | 3,242 ms |
| today, pre-GC | 7.71/s | 6,364 ms |
| post-GC | 8.85/s | 5,537 ms |
| **post-restart + 3G mem** | **9.1/s** | 5,571 ms |

GC didn't help, memory bump didn't help, restart didn't help — **all three ruled out empirically.** The regression is persistent (~40% below baseline) and CPU-starvation-driven. (And the 9.1/s is if anything slightly *pessimistic* — it ran while the restart's provide-backlog catch-up was re-announcing all 76k CIDs, eating ~half the core.)

This also finally explains **19.2 (15/s) vs now (9/s) on the identical 1-CPU cap**: in March the provide set was ~hundreds (negligible background CPU → near-full core served pins); now 76k CIDs consume ~half the core. Same cap, less of it available.

## Bottom line for your original question

The recent API/SDK changes did **not** regress the upload path — server-side pin is the cost, and it's Kubo-local. The throughput drop is an **infrastructure scaling issue**: Kubo's provider on a capped core as the pinned set grew ~100×.

## Fix levers (now that memory/GC/restart are out)

1. **Tune the reprovider** (highest leverage, object-count-aware): config is default (`{}`) = strategy "all" (announces *every* block). Switch to `Reprovider.Strategy: "roots"` (announce only pin roots → ~76k down to ~18k) and/or lengthen `Reprovider.Interval`. Or **delegate providing to someguy** (it's the accelerated-DHT sidecar that exists for exactly this) so Kubo's core stops doing DHT announces.
2. **More CPU for Kubo** — raise the 1.0 cap and/or a bigger box. But providing keeps growing with objects, so do #1 regardless.
3. **Shrink the pinned set** — much of the 17.9k is dev/test churn (staging); a cleanup cuts the providing workload.
4. **Revert the 3G mem bump** — it didn't help (idle mem 243 MiB); no reason to make it permanent. It auto-reverts on next deploy anyway.

Want me to **capture this as a dedicated perf issue** (Kubo reprovider scaling → upload throughput regression, with these numbers and the reprovider-tuning fix), and/or **revert the 3G cap** on staging now?

The three-point local comparison (Phase 19.2) provides matched-environment data; the staging CI data provides production-representative data.
85

87	
88	IPNS publish storm with Someguy sidecar (5 clients x 50 folder create-rename-delete cycles = 750 ops):
89

91	| -------------------------- | -------- | ----------- | ---------------- | ---------------- | ------ |

97	
98	### 1.4 Server-Side Pin Latency (Prometheus, Post-Optimization)
99	
100	Kubo pin latency distribution captured from staging after 20,944 pin operations (pebbleds datastore):
101	
102	| Bucket   | Count  | Cumulative % |
103	| -------- | ------ | ------------ |
104	| <= 10ms  | 28     | 0.1%         |
105	| <= 50ms  | 181    | 0.9%         |
106	| <= 100ms | 564    | 2.7%         |
107	| <= 250ms | 2,042  | 9.7%         |
108	| <= 500ms | 4,944  | 23.6%        |

110	| <= 2.5s  | 17,477 | 83.4%        |
111	| <= 5s    | 20,898 | 99.8%        |
112	| <= 10s   | 20,944 | 100%         |
113	
114	**Mean pin latency:** 1.37s (down from 1.73s pre-optimization, -20.8%)
115	
116	---
117	
118	## 2. Infrastructure Bottlenecks
119	
120	### 2.1 Kubo IPFS Node
121	
122	Kubo's `pin add` operation is the **dominant bottleneck**, consuming ~95% of upload endpoint latency. Each `uploadFile` SDK call requires 3 sequential pin operations (ciphertext, file metadata, folder metadata), totaling ~4-5s server-side at mean.
123	
124	**Optimization impact (pebbleds datastore):**
125	
126	| Metric               | flatfs (pre) | pebbleds (post) | Change     |
127	| -------------------- | ------------ | --------------- | ---------- |
128	| Pin mean latency     | 1.73s        | 1.37s           | -20.8%     |
129	| Pin p50 (estimated)  | ~1.7s        | ~1.0s           | -41%       |
130	| IPNS publish mean    | ~120ms       | ~50ms           | -58%       |
131	| 75-client errors     | 10           | 0               | Eliminated |
132	| 75-client throughput | 2.44 ops/s   | 3.51 ops/s      | +43.9%     |
133	
134	Concurrent pins from multiple clients cause contention on the Kubo datastore. At 50 clients, throughput plateaus at ~3.4-3.7 ops/s locally and ~15-19 ops/s on staging. At 75 clients with flatfs, errors begin appearing; pebbleds eliminates this failure mode entirely.
135	
136	**Memory and CPU:** Kubo uses Go's goroutine scheduler. Pin operations are I/O-bound on the datastore. The pebbleds LSM-tree datastore batches writes, reducing I/O contention under concurrent load.
137	
138	### 2.2 PostgreSQL
139	
140	Auth lookups, IPNS record cache reads/writes, and vault operations are fast:
141	
142	| Operation        | Mean Latency |
143	| ---------------- | ------------ |
144	| Vault lookup     | < 5ms        |
145	| Quota check      | < 5ms        |
146	| IPNS DB resolve  | 23-36ms      |
147	| IPNS DB upsert   | ~50ms        |
148	| Auth login (JWT) | 104-155ms    |
149	
150	PostgreSQL is **not the bottleneck** at current scale. The `folder_ipns` table grows linearly with `users x folders`, but even at 200 concurrent clients, DB operations remain sub-100ms.
151	
152	**Connection pooling:** TypeORM manages the connection pool. Default pool size handles current concurrency levels without exhaustion.
153	
154	### 2.3 API Server (NestJS)
155	
156	Request processing overhead is minimal (~5-10ms per request excluding downstream IPFS/IPNS calls). The API server acts primarily as a pass-through to Kubo for IPFS operations and to PostgreSQL for IPNS record management.
157	
158	- **Rate limiting:** ThrottlerGuard protects against abuse. Load tests bypass throttling via `THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET` in test mode.
159	- **Connection handling:** NestJS handles concurrent HTTP connections efficiently. No observed issues at 200 concurrent clients.
160	- **CPU:** Not a bottleneck. Server-side processing time per request is dominated by Kubo pin latency, not application logic.
161	
162	### 2.4 Redis
163	
164	Used for rate limiting state and session management. Sub-millisecond operations. Not a bottleneck at any observed concurrency level.
165	
166	### 2.5 Someguy (Delegated Routing Sidecar)
167	
168	IPNS publish DHT propagation happens asynchronously and does not block client responses. DHT propagation latency:
169	
170	| Outcome | Mean  | Count   | Error Rate |
171	| ------- | ----- | ------- | ---------- |
172	| Success | 838ms | 147,285 | --         |
173	| Error   | 17.2s | 324     | 0.22%      |
174	
175	DHT propagation errors do not affect client-facing operations (fire-and-forget). Someguy's warm DHT is critical for IPNS resolution performance in non-API contexts (recovery tool, TEE republishing).
176	
177	---
178	
179	## 3. Scaling Recommendations
180	
181	### 3.1 When to Scale
182	
183	| Signal                                     | Threshold              | Action                                     |
184	| ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
185	| Upload p95 > 5s consistently (staging)     | Kubo pin contention    | Add second Kubo node or upgrade hardware   |
186	| Upload p95 > 15s consistently (staging)    | Kubo saturated         | Kubo cluster mode or dedicated pin workers |
187	| API response time p95 > 500ms (non-IPFS)   | API CPU bound          | Add API replica behind load balancer       |
188	| PostgreSQL connections > 80% pool          | DB saturated           | Increase pool size or add read replica     |
189	| Kubo datastore > 80% disk                  | Storage full           | Expand volume or enable garbage collection |
190	| IPNS publish queue depth > 100             | Publish backlog        | Tune Kubo worker concurrency               |
191	| Mixed workload error rate > 1%             | Infrastructure ceiling | Scale horizontally (Kubo + API)            |
192	| Throughput plateaus despite adding clients | Single-node ceiling    | Horizontal scaling required                |
193	
194	### 3.2 How to Scale
195	
196	**Kubo IPFS Node:**
197	
198	- **Vertical:** Increase CPU/RAM/SSD. Pebbleds datastore benefits significantly from faster I/O. Move from HDD to NVMe SSD for pin operations.
199	- **Horizontal:** Run multiple Kubo nodes behind the API. Each API instance pins to a designated Kubo node. Requires content routing coordination (IPFS Cluster or custom routing).
200	- **Cluster mode:** [IPFS Cluster](https://cluster.ipfs.io/) adds pinning coordination but introduces operational complexity. Recommended only when single-node Kubo reaches sustained saturation.
201	
202	**API Server (NestJS):**
203	
204	- The API is stateless (session state in Redis, no in-memory state). Adding replicas behind Caddy or nginx is straightforward.
205	- Ensure all replicas share the same Redis instance for rate limiting and session consistency.
206	- Database connection pool per replica needs coordination (total connections = replicas x pool_size).
207	
208	**PostgreSQL:**
209	
210	- **Read replicas:** IPNS cache reads can be directed to read replicas. Write scaling is unnecessary at current volume.
211	- **Connection pooling:** Use PgBouncer if connection count exceeds PostgreSQL's `max_connections`.
212	- **Sharding:** Premature for a tech demo. Only consider if user count exceeds ~100,000.
213	
214	**TEE Republishing:**
215	
216	- Independent scaling path. Add TEE workers to increase IPNS republish batch throughput.
217	- Each TEE worker processes a batch of IPNS names every 6 hours.
218	- Batch duration grows linearly with IPNS name count. Monitor `cipherbox_republish_batch_duration_seconds`.
219	
220	---
221	
222	## 4. Growth Projections
223	
224	### 4.1 Storage Growth
225	
226	All files are encrypted with unique keys, so IPFS deduplication does not apply.
227	
228	**Formula:**
229	
230	```text
231	storage_bytes = users * avg_files_per_user * avg_encrypted_file_size * 1.05
232	```
233	
234	The 1.05 multiplier accounts for ~5% metadata overhead (file metadata CIDs, folder metadata CIDs, IPNS records).
235	
236	| Users  | Files/User | Avg File Size | IPFS Storage | Monthly Growth (10 files/user/mo) |
237	| ------ | ---------- | ------------- | ------------ | --------------------------------- |
238	| 100    | 100        | 500KB         | ~5 GB        | ~500 MB/mo                        |
239	| 1,000  | 100        | 500KB         | ~50 GB       | ~5 GB/mo                          |
240	| 10,000 | 100        | 500KB         | ~500 GB      | ~50 GB/mo                         |
241	| 1,000  | 100        | 5MB           | ~500 GB      | ~50 GB/mo                         |
242	
243	### 4.2 IPNS Name Growth
244	
245	Each user has:
246	
247	- 1 vault blob IPNS name
248	- N folder IPNS names (1 per folder including root)
249	- M file IPNS names (1 per file)
250	
251	**Formula:**
252	
253	```text
254	ipns_names = users * (1 + avg_folders_per_user + avg_files_per_user)
255	```
256	
257	| Users  | Folders/User | Files/User | Total IPNS Names | TEE Republish Batch Size |
258	| ------ | ------------ | ---------- | ---------------- | ------------------------ |
259	| 100    | 10           | 100        | ~11,100          | ~11,100 every 6h         |
260	| 1,000  | 10           | 100        | ~111,000         | ~111,000 every 6h        |
261	| 10,000 | 10           | 100        | ~1,110,000       | ~1,110,000 every 6h      |
262	
263	TEE republish batch duration scales linearly with IPNS name count. At current Someguy publish throughput (~15 ops/s), 111,000 names would take ~2 hours to republish -- within the 6-hour window. At 1.1M names, multiple TEE workers or batching optimizations would be needed.
264	
265	### 4.3 Database Growth
266	
267	| Table         | Growth Driver             | Rows at 1,000 Users | Rows at 10,000 Users |
268	| ------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------- | -------------------- |
269	| users         | 1 per user                | 1,000               | 10,000               |
270	| vaults        | 1 per user                | 1,000               | 10,000               |
271	| folder_ipns   | users x (folders + files) | ~111,000            | ~1,110,000           |
272	| device_tokens | users x avg_devices       | ~2,000              | ~20,000              |
273	
274	The `folder_ipns` table is the largest growth driver. With proper indexing (already in place on `user_id`, with a unique constraint on `(user_id, ipns_name)`), queries remain efficient at millions of rows.
275	
276	### 4.4 Cost Estimates (Single Server Deployment)
277	
278	These are rough estimates for a self-hosted tech demo deployment, not production SLAs.
279	
280	| Component     | 100 Users      | 1,000 Users     | 10,000 Users     |
281	| ------------- | -------------- | --------------- | ---------------- |
282	| VPS (CPU/RAM) | $10-20/mo      | $40-80/mo       | $150-300/mo      |
283	| Storage (SSD) | $5/mo (50GB)   | $25/mo (250GB)  | $100/mo (1TB)    |
284	| Bandwidth     | $5/mo          | $20/mo          | $100/mo          |
285	| Domain/SSL    | $15/yr         | $15/yr          | $15/yr           |
286	| **Total**     | **~$20-30/mo** | **~$85-125/mo** | **~$350-500/mo** |
287	
288	**Notes:**
289	
290	- VPS pricing based on Hostinger/Hetzner tier estimates
291	- Storage assumes SSD volumes at ~$0.10/GB/mo
292	- Bandwidth depends heavily on download patterns and provider egress pricing
293	- Does not include TEE infrastructure costs (Phala Cloud pricing varies)
294	
295	---
296	
297	## 5. Load Test Thresholds
298	
299	Automated pass/fail thresholds are defined in `tests/load/src/harness/thresholds.ts` and integrated into all 8 load test scenarios. Thresholds are 2-3x observed baselines to avoid CI flakiness while still catching significant regressions.
300	
301	| Scenario           | Operation    | p95 Threshold | Error Rate Max | Rationale                                 |
302	| ------------------ | ------------ | ------------- | -------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
303	| upload-throughput  | uploadFile   | 10,000ms      | 5%             | 19.2 p95 was 2,841ms at 5 clients (~3.5x) |
304	| mixed-workload     | uploadFile   | 10,000ms      | 10%            | Mixed has higher error rate historically  |
305	| mixed-workload     | createFolder | 5,000ms       | 10%            | 19.2 p95 was 936ms at 5 clients (~5x)     |
306	| ipns-publish-storm | createFolder | 10,000ms      | 10%            | IPNS contention scenario, high variance   |
307	| sustained-load     | uploadFile   | 10,000ms      | 5%             | Same as upload-throughput                 |
308	| sustained-load     | createFolder | 5,000ms       | 5%             | Folder ops should stay fast               |
309	| spike-test (burst) | uploadFile   | 15,000ms      | 15%            | Spike: intentional overload               |
310	| spike-test (burst) | createFolder | 15,000ms      | 15%            | Spike: intentional overload               |
311	
312	**How thresholds work:**
313	
314	1. Each scenario runs its workload and collects `OperationMetrics` via `aggregateAndReport()`
315	2. `checkThresholds()` compares observed p95 latency and error rate against the threshold table
316	3. If any threshold is breached, the test fails with a descriptive violation message listing the operation, observed value, and threshold
317	4. The CI workflow (`load-test.yml`) runs via `workflow_dispatch` (manual trigger), not on every push
318	
319	**Updating thresholds:** When baselines shift significantly (new infrastructure, new optimizations), update the threshold values in each scenario file. Keep thresholds at 2-3x observed values to maintain a buffer against normal variance.
320	
321	---
322	
323	## 7. Retention Consequence of BYO Advisory Rows
324	
325	### 7.1 Background
326	
327	CipherBox supports two storage modes for each file CID in `pinned_cids`:
328	
329	- **Hosted rows**: CIDs pinned via the CipherBox relay (`isByoUser = false`). The CipherBox
330	  Kubo node physically holds the content.
331	- **BYO advisory rows**: CIDs registered by BYO-IPFS users (`isByoUser = true`). These rows
332	  track what the user claims is pinned on their own infrastructure; the CipherBox Kubo node
333	  does NOT hold these CIDs.
334	
335	### 7.2 The Retention Consequence
336	
337	The `guardedUnpin` refcount query counts ALL `pinned_cids` rows for a given CID regardless of
338	origin — both hosted and BYO advisory rows contribute to the refcount (D-07 design, WR-07
339	disposition: accepted).
340	
341	**Consequence:** If a BYO advisory row exists for a CID that is also held by the CipherBox Kubo
342	node (hosted), deleting the hosted row will NOT trigger a physical unpin of the CID from Kubo
343	until the BYO advisory row is also removed. The CID is retained in Kubo for as long as any BYO
344	advisory row references it.
345	
346	**When this occurs:**
347	
348	1. User A uploads a file via the CipherBox relay (hosted `pinned_cids` row created).
349	2. User B (BYO-IPFS mode) registers the same CID (advisory `pinned_cids` row created).
350	3. User A deletes their file — their hosted row is removed and their quota is decremented
351	   immediately (D-03), but the CID remains pinned in Kubo because User B's advisory row
352	   keeps the refcount above zero.
353	4. Kubo storage is freed only when User B also removes their advisory row.
354	
355	**Impact on capacity planning:** In environments with significant BYO-IPFS usage, Kubo storage
356	consumption may exceed what is attributable to hosted users alone. Monitor
357	`cipherbox_pending_unpin_queue_depth` and `cipherbox_drift_orphaned_pins_total` for divergence
358	between DB-accounted and Kubo-actual pin counts.
359	
360	**Operator action:** No action is required — this is intentional design. If an operator needs
361	to reclaim Kubo storage held by a BYO-referenced CID, they must first remove the BYO advisory
362	row (e.g., by having the BYO user delete their reference), which will allow the next
363	`drain-pending-unpins` BullMQ run to physically unpin it.
364	
365	---
366	
367	## 6. References
368	
369	### Baseline Documents
370	
371	- `.planning/baselines/18-performance-baselines.md` -- Server-side Prometheus baselines (Phase 18)
372	- `.planning/baselines/19-someguy-ipns-baselines.md` -- IPNS resolution baselines with Someguy sidecar (Phase 19)
373	- `.planning/baselines/19.2-pre-optimization-baselines.md` -- Upload baselines before concurrent pins + pebbleds
374	- `.planning/baselines/19.2-post-optimization-baselines.md` -- Comprehensive post-optimization baselines with three-point comparison
375	
376	### Load Test Infrastructure
377	
378	- `tests/load/src/harness/thresholds.ts` -- Threshold checking module (ThresholdConfig, checkThresholds)
379	- `tests/load/src/harness/metrics.ts` -- MetricsCollector with percentile calculation
380	- `tests/load/src/harness/client-pool.ts` -- Multi-client pool management
381	- `tests/load/src/scenarios/` -- 8 load test scenarios with threshold assertions
382	- `.github/workflows/load-test.yml` -- CI workflow for staging load tests
383	
384	### Architecture
385	
386	- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` -- System architecture overview
387	- `docs/METADATA_SCHEMAS.md` -- Metadata schema reference
388	
389	---
390

# CipherBox Capacity Model

> Observed performance limits, infrastructure bottlenecks, and scaling recommendations.
> Based on baseline data captured during Phases 18, 19, 19.2, and 22.
>
> **Last updated:** 2026-03-25
> **Environment:** Single API server + single Kubo node + PostgreSQL

## Table of Contents

1. [Observed Limits](#1-observed-limits)
2. [Infrastructure Bottlenecks](#2-infrastructure-bottlenecks)
3. [Scaling Recommendations](#3-scaling-recommendations)
4. [Growth Projections](#4-growth-projections)
5. [Load Test Thresholds](#5-load-test-thresholds)
6. [References](#6-references)

---

## 1. Observed Limits

### 1.1 Single-User Performance (Phase 18)

Client-side round-trip timings captured against staging (4 vCPU, 8GB RAM VPS) using `curl` with a 10KB test file:

| Operation           | p50   | p95   | p99   |
| ------------------- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| IPNS Resolve        | 147ms | 224ms | 278ms |
| IPFS Pin (upload)   | 138ms | 218ms | 227ms |
| IPFS Cat (download) | 133ms | 215ms | 219ms |

Server-side Prometheus histograms (cumulative across benchmark + 5-client load test):

| Operation    | Source  | Count | p50   | p95   | p99   | Mean  |
| ------------ | ------- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| IPNS Publish | --      | 1,367 | 180ms | 519ms | 904ms | 196ms |
| IPNS Resolve | network | 529   | 135ms | 284ms | 488ms | 126ms |
| IPNS Resolve | db      | 84    | 35ms  | 93ms  | 187ms | 36ms  |
| IPFS Pin     | --      | 1,923 | 8ms   | 18ms  | 31ms  | 8ms   |
| IPFS Cat     | --      | 704   | 2ms   | 5ms   | 9ms   | 2ms   |

HTTP API response times (server-side, routes with >= 10 requests):

| Route                    | Count | p50   | p95   | p99   |
| ------------------------ | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| POST /ipfs/upload [201]  | 1,923 | 8ms   | 45ms  | 50ms  |
| GET /ipfs/:cid [200]     | 704   | 5ms   | 10ms  | 10ms  |
| GET /ipns/resolve [200]  | 852   | 50ms  | 245ms | 467ms |
| POST /ipns/publish [201] | 621   | 165ms | 477ms | 871ms |
| POST /auth/login [200]   | 14    | 155ms | 240ms | 248ms |
| GET /vault [200]         | 12    | 5ms   | 9ms   | 10ms  |
| GET /vault/quota [200]   | 838   | 5ms   | 9ms   | 10ms  |

### 1.2 Concurrent User Scaling (Phase 19.2)

Upload throughput scaling measured with SDK-based load test harness against local infrastructure (pebbleds datastore, concurrent SDK pins):

| Clients | uploadFile p50 | uploadFile p95 | Throughput | Errors |
| ------- | -------------- | -------------- | ---------- | ------ |
| 1       | 131ms          | 287ms          | 6.36 ops/s | 0      |
| 5       | 1,016ms        | 1,871ms        | 4.97 ops/s | 0      |
| 10      | 2,499ms        | 3,768ms        | 3.95 ops/s | 0      |
| 20      | 5,897ms        | 8,806ms        | 3.43 ops/s | 0      |
| 50      | 14,789ms       | 19,315ms       | 3.36 ops/s | 0      |
| 75      | 21,969ms       | 25,316ms       | 3.51 ops/s | 0      |

Staging CI load tests (GitHub Actions runner against staging VPS, post-optimization):

| Clients | uploadFile p50 | uploadFile p95 | Throughput  | Errors | Error Rate |
| ------- | -------------- | -------------- | ----------- | ------ | ---------- |
| 50      | 3,242ms        | 4,615ms        | 15.10 ops/s | 0      | 0%         |
| 100     | 5,300ms        | 8,300ms        | 18.76 ops/s | 0      | 0%         |
| 200     | 10,500ms       | 15,500ms       | 19.22 ops/s | 58     | 1.5%       |

Mixed workload scaling (staging, weighted mix of CRUD operations):

| Clients | createFolder p50 | uploadFile p50 | Throughput  | Errors |
| ------- | ---------------- | -------------- | ----------- | ------ |
| 5       | 511ms            | 613ms          | 9.32 ops/s  | 0      |
| 50      | 2,000ms          | 2,700ms        | 22.86 ops/s | 0      |
| 100     | 3,700ms          | 5,100ms        | 24.05 ops/s | 0      |
| 200     | 6,200ms          | 8,800ms        | 28.50 ops/s | 4      |

**Environment caveat:** Local and staging measurements are not directly comparable. Local infrastructure has different network characteristics, CPU, and I/O profiles than the staging VPS. The three-point local comparison (Phase 19.2) provides matched-environment data; the staging CI data provides production-representative data.

| Local (someguy, cold DHT)  | 89.3s    | 8.39 ops/s  | 728ms            | 1,070ms          | 0      |

## 2. Infrastructure Bottlenecks

### 2.1 Kubo IPFS Node

Kubo's `pin add` operation is the **dominant bottleneck**, consuming ~95% of upload endpoint latency. Each `uploadFile` SDK call requires 3 sequential pin operations (ciphertext, file metadata, folder metadata), totaling ~4-5s server-side at mean.

**Optimization impact (pebbleds datastore):**

| Metric               | flatfs (pre) | pebbleds (post) | Change     |
| -------------------- | ------------ | --------------- | ---------- |
| Pin mean latency     | 1.73s        | 1.37s           | -20.8%     |
| Pin p50 (estimated)  | ~1.7s        | ~1.0s           | -41%       |
| IPNS publish mean    | ~120ms       | ~50ms           | -58%       |
| 75-client errors     | 10           | 0               | Eliminated |
| 75-client throughput | 2.44 ops/s   | 3.51 ops/s      | +43.9%     |

Concurrent pins from multiple clients cause contention on the Kubo datastore. At 50 clients, throughput plateaus at ~3.4-3.7 ops/s locally and ~15-19 ops/s on staging. At 75 clients with flatfs, errors begin appearing; pebbleds eliminates this failure mode entirely.

**Memory and CPU:** Kubo uses Go's goroutine scheduler. Pin operations are I/O-bound on the datastore. The pebbleds LSM-tree datastore batches writes, reducing I/O contention under concurrent load.

### 2.2 PostgreSQL

Auth lookups, IPNS record cache reads/writes, and vault operations are fast:

| Operation        | Mean Latency |
| ---------------- | ------------ |
| Vault lookup     | < 5ms        |
| Quota check      | < 5ms        |
| IPNS DB resolve  | 23-36ms      |
| IPNS DB upsert   | ~50ms        |
| Auth login (JWT) | 104-155ms    |

PostgreSQL is **not the bottleneck** at current scale. The `folder_ipns` table grows linearly with `users x folders`, but even at 200 concurrent clients, DB operations remain sub-100ms.

**Connection pooling:** TypeORM manages the connection pool. Default pool size handles current concurrency levels without exhaustion.

### 2.3 API Server (NestJS)

Request processing overhead is minimal (~5-10ms per request excluding downstream IPFS/IPNS calls). The API server acts primarily as a pass-through to Kubo for IPFS operations and to PostgreSQL for IPNS record management.

- **Rate limiting:** ThrottlerGuard protects against abuse. Load tests bypass throttling via `THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET` in test mode.
- **Connection handling:** NestJS handles concurrent HTTP connections efficiently. No observed issues at 200 concurrent clients.
- **CPU:** Not a bottleneck. Server-side processing time per request is dominated by Kubo pin latency, not application logic.

### 2.4 Redis

Used for rate limiting state and session management. Sub-millisecond operations. Not a bottleneck at any observed concurrency level.

### 2.5 Someguy (Delegated Routing Sidecar)

IPNS publish DHT propagation happens asynchronously and does not block client responses. DHT propagation latency:

| Outcome | Mean  | Count   | Error Rate |
| ------- | ----- | ------- | ---------- |
| Success | 838ms | 147,285 | --         |
| Error   | 17.2s | 324     | 0.22%      |

DHT propagation errors do not affect client-facing operations (fire-and-forget). Someguy's warm DHT is critical for IPNS resolution performance in non-API contexts (recovery tool, TEE republishing).
