# CipherBox Capacity Model

> Observed performance limits, infrastructure bottlenecks, and scaling recommendations.
> Based on baseline data captured during Phases 18, 19, 19.2, and 22.
>
> **Last updated:** 2026-03-25
> **Environment:** Single API server + single Kubo node + PostgreSQL

## Table of Contents

1. [Observed Limits](#1-observed-limits)
2. [Infrastructure Bottlenecks](#2-infrastructure-bottlenecks)
3. [Scaling Recommendations](#3-scaling-recommendations)
4. [Growth Projections](#4-growth-projections)
5. [Load Test Thresholds](#5-load-test-thresholds)
6. [References](#6-references)

---

## 1. Observed Limits

### 1.1 Single-User Performance (Phase 18)

Client-side round-trip timings captured against staging (4 vCPU, 8GB RAM VPS) using `curl` with a 10KB test file:

| Operation           | p50   | p95   | p99   |
| ------------------- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| IPNS Resolve        | 147ms | 224ms | 278ms |
| IPFS Pin (upload)   | 138ms | 218ms | 227ms |
| IPFS Cat (download) | 133ms | 215ms | 219ms |

Server-side Prometheus histograms (cumulative across benchmark + 5-client load test):

| Operation    | Source  | Count | p50   | p95   | p99   | Mean  |
| ------------ | ------- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| IPNS Publish | --      | 1,367 | 180ms | 519ms | 904ms | 196ms |
| IPNS Resolve | network | 529   | 135ms | 284ms | 488ms | 126ms |
| IPNS Resolve | db      | 84    | 35ms  | 93ms  | 187ms | 36ms  |
| IPFS Pin     | --      | 1,923 | 8ms   | 18ms  | 31ms  | 8ms   |
| IPFS Cat     | --      | 704   | 2ms   | 5ms   | 9ms   | 2ms   |

HTTP API response times (server-side, routes with >= 10 requests):

| Route                    | Count | p50   | p95   | p99   |
| ------------------------ | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| POST /ipfs/upload [201]  | 1,923 | 8ms   | 45ms  | 50ms  |
| GET /ipfs/:cid [200]     | 704   | 5ms   | 10ms  | 10ms  |
| GET /ipns/resolve [200]  | 852   | 50ms  | 245ms | 467ms |
| POST /ipns/publish [201] | 621   | 165ms | 477ms | 871ms |
| POST /auth/login [200]   | 14    | 155ms | 240ms | 248ms |
| GET /vault [200]         | 12    | 5ms   | 9ms   | 10ms  |
| GET /vault/quota [200]   | 838   | 5ms   | 9ms   | 10ms  |

### 1.2 Concurrent User Scaling (Phase 19.2)

Upload throughput scaling measured with SDK-based load test harness against local infrastructure (pebbleds datastore, concurrent SDK pins):

| Clients | uploadFile p50 | uploadFile p95 | Throughput | Errors |
| ------- | -------------- | -------------- | ---------- | ------ |
| 1       | 131ms          | 287ms          | 6.36 ops/s | 0      |
| 5       | 1,016ms        | 1,871ms        | 4.97 ops/s | 0      |
| 10      | 2,499ms        | 3,768ms        | 3.95 ops/s | 0      |
| 20      | 5,897ms        | 8,806ms        | 3.43 ops/s | 0      |
| 50      | 14,789ms       | 19,315ms       | 3.36 ops/s | 0      |
| 75      | 21,969ms       | 25,316ms       | 3.51 ops/s | 0      |

Staging CI load tests (GitHub Actions runner against staging VPS, post-optimization):

| Clients | uploadFile p50 | uploadFile p95 | Throughput  | Errors | Error Rate |
| ------- | -------------- | -------------- | ----------- | ------ | ---------- |
| 50      | 3,242ms        | 4,615ms        | 15.10 ops/s | 0      | 0%         |
| 100     | 5,300ms        | 8,300ms        | 18.76 ops/s | 0      | 0%         |
| 200     | 10,500ms       | 15,500ms       | 19.22 ops/s | 58     | 1.5%       |

Mixed workload scaling (staging, weighted mix of CRUD operations):

| Clients | createFolder p50 | uploadFile p50 | Throughput  | Errors |
| ------- | ---------------- | -------------- | ----------- | ------ |
| 5       | 511ms            | 613ms          | 9.32 ops/s  | 0      |
| 50      | 2,000ms          | 2,700ms        | 22.86 ops/s | 0      |
| 100     | 3,700ms          | 5,100ms        | 24.05 ops/s | 0      |
| 200     | 6,200ms          | 8,800ms        | 28.50 ops/s | 4      |

**Environment caveat:** Local and staging measurements are not directly comparable. Local infrastructure has different network characteristics, CPU, and I/O profiles than the staging VPS. The three-point local comparison (Phase 19.2) provides matched-environment data; the staging CI data provides production-representative data.

### 1.3 IPNS Publish Throughput (Phase 19)

IPNS publish storm with Someguy sidecar (5 clients x 50 folder create-rename-delete cycles = 750 ops):

| Environment                | Duration | Throughput  | createFolder p50 | createFolder p95 | Errors |
| -------------------------- | -------- | ----------- | ---------------- | ---------------- | ------ |
| Staging (warm DHT, 8h)     | 49.1s    | 15.28 ops/s | 468ms            | 848ms            | 0      |
| Local (delegated-ipfs.dev) | 69.7s    | 10.75 ops/s | 606ms            | 1,220ms          | 0      |
| Local (someguy, cold DHT)  | 89.3s    | 8.39 ops/s  | 728ms            | 1,070ms          | 0      |

**Key finding:** DHT warm-up matters significantly. Staging someguy (8h uptime) is ~2x faster than local someguy with a cold DHT (10min uptime).

### 1.4 Server-Side Pin Latency (Prometheus, Post-Optimization)

Kubo pin latency distribution captured from staging after 20,944 pin operations (pebbleds datastore):

| Bucket   | Count  | Cumulative % |
| -------- | ------ | ------------ |
| <= 10ms  | 28     | 0.1%         |
| <= 50ms  | 181    | 0.9%         |
| <= 100ms | 564    | 2.7%         |
| <= 250ms | 2,042  | 9.7%         |
| <= 500ms | 4,944  | 23.6%        |
| <= 1s    | 9,341  | 44.6%        |
| <= 2.5s  | 17,477 | 83.4%        |
| <= 5s    | 20,898 | 99.8%        |
| <= 10s   | 20,944 | 100%         |

**Mean pin latency:** 1.37s (down from 1.73s pre-optimization, -20.8%)

---

## 2. Infrastructure Bottlenecks

### 2.1 Kubo IPFS Node

Kubo's `pin add` operation is the **dominant bottleneck**, consuming ~95% of upload endpoint latency. Each `uploadFile` SDK call requires 3 sequential pin operations (ciphertext, file metadata, folder metadata), totaling ~4-5s server-side at mean.

**Optimization impact (pebbleds datastore):**

| Metric               | flatfs (pre) | pebbleds (post) | Change     |
| -------------------- | ------------ | --------------- | ---------- |
| Pin mean latency     | 1.73s        | 1.37s           | -20.8%     |
| Pin p50 (estimated)  | ~1.7s        | ~1.0s           | -41%       |
| IPNS publish mean    | ~120ms       | ~50ms           | -58%       |
| 75-client errors     | 10           | 0               | Eliminated |
| 75-client throughput | 2.44 ops/s   | 3.51 ops/s      | +43.9%     |

Concurrent pins from multiple clients cause contention on the Kubo datastore. At 50 clients, throughput plateaus at ~3.4-3.7 ops/s locally and ~15-19 ops/s on staging. At 75 clients with flatfs, errors begin appearing; pebbleds eliminates this failure mode entirely.

**Memory and CPU:** Kubo uses Go's goroutine scheduler. Pin operations are I/O-bound on the datastore. The pebbleds LSM-tree datastore batches writes, reducing I/O contention under concurrent load.

### 2.2 PostgreSQL

Auth lookups, IPNS record cache reads/writes, and vault operations are fast:

| Operation        | Mean Latency |
| ---------------- | ------------ |
| Vault lookup     | < 5ms        |
| Quota check      | < 5ms        |
| IPNS DB resolve  | 23-36ms      |
| IPNS DB upsert   | ~50ms        |
| Auth login (JWT) | 104-155ms    |

PostgreSQL is **not the bottleneck** at current scale. The `folder_ipns` table grows linearly with `users x folders`, but even at 200 concurrent clients, DB operations remain sub-100ms.

**Connection pooling:** TypeORM manages the connection pool. Default pool size handles current concurrency levels without exhaustion.

### 2.3 API Server (NestJS)

Request processing overhead is minimal (~5-10ms per request excluding downstream IPFS/IPNS calls). The API server acts primarily as a pass-through to Kubo for IPFS operations and to PostgreSQL for IPNS record management.

- **Rate limiting:** ThrottlerGuard protects against abuse. Load tests bypass throttling via `THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET` in test mode.
- **Connection handling:** NestJS handles concurrent HTTP connections efficiently. No observed issues at 200 concurrent clients.
- **CPU:** Not a bottleneck. Server-side processing time per request is dominated by Kubo pin latency, not application logic.

### 2.4 Redis

Used for rate limiting state and session management. Sub-millisecond operations. Not a bottleneck at any observed concurrency level.

### 2.5 Someguy (Delegated Routing Sidecar)

IPNS publish DHT propagation happens asynchronously and does not block client responses. DHT propagation latency:

| Outcome | Mean  | Count   | Error Rate |
| ------- | ----- | ------- | ---------- |
| Success | 838ms | 147,285 | --         |
| Error   | 17.2s | 324     | 0.22%      |

DHT propagation errors do not affect client-facing operations (fire-and-forget). Someguy's warm DHT is critical for IPNS resolution performance in non-API contexts (recovery tool, TEE republishing).

---

## 3. Scaling Recommendations

### 3.1 When to Scale

| Signal                                     | Threshold              | Action                                     |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Upload p95 > 5s consistently (staging)     | Kubo pin contention    | Add second Kubo node or upgrade hardware   |
| Upload p95 > 15s consistently (staging)    | Kubo saturated         | Kubo cluster mode or dedicated pin workers |
| API response time p95 > 500ms (non-IPFS)   | API CPU bound          | Add API replica behind load balancer       |
| PostgreSQL connections > 80% pool          | DB saturated           | Increase pool size or add read replica     |
| Kubo datastore > 80% disk                  | Storage full           | Expand volume or enable garbage collection |
| IPNS publish queue depth > 100             | Publish backlog        | Tune Kubo worker concurrency               |
| Mixed workload error rate > 1%             | Infrastructure ceiling | Scale horizontally (Kubo + API)            |
| Throughput plateaus despite adding clients | Single-node ceiling    | Horizontal scaling required                |

### 3.2 How to Scale

**Kubo IPFS Node:**

- **Vertical:** Increase CPU/RAM/SSD. Pebbleds datastore benefits significantly from faster I/O. Move from HDD to NVMe SSD for pin operations.
- **Horizontal:** Run multiple Kubo nodes behind the API. Each API instance pins to a designated Kubo node. Requires content routing coordination (IPFS Cluster or custom routing).
- **Cluster mode:** [IPFS Cluster](https://cluster.ipfs.io/) adds pinning coordination but introduces operational complexity. Recommended only when single-node Kubo reaches sustained saturation.

**API Server (NestJS):**

- The API is stateless (session state in Redis, no in-memory state). Adding replicas behind Caddy or nginx is straightforward.
- Ensure all replicas share the same Redis instance for rate limiting and session consistency.
- Database connection pool per replica needs coordination (total connections = replicas x pool_size).

**PostgreSQL:**

- **Read replicas:** IPNS cache reads can be directed to read replicas. Write scaling is unnecessary at current volume.
- **Connection pooling:** Use PgBouncer if connection count exceeds PostgreSQL's `max_connections`.
- **Sharding:** Premature for a tech demo. Only consider if user count exceeds ~100,000.

**TEE Republishing:**

- Independent scaling path. Add TEE workers to increase IPNS republish batch throughput.
- Each TEE worker processes a batch of IPNS names every 6 hours.
- Batch duration grows linearly with IPNS name count. Monitor `cipherbox_republish_batch_duration_seconds`.

---

## 4. Growth Projections

### 4.1 Storage Growth

All files are encrypted with unique keys, so IPFS deduplication does not apply.

**Formula:**

```text
storage_bytes = users * avg_files_per_user * avg_encrypted_file_size * 1.05
```

The 1.05 multiplier accounts for ~5% metadata overhead (file metadata CIDs, folder metadata CIDs, IPNS records).

| Users  | Files/User | Avg File Size | IPFS Storage | Monthly Growth (10 files/user/mo) |
| ------ | ---------- | ------------- | ------------ | --------------------------------- |
| 100    | 100        | 500KB         | ~5 GB        | ~500 MB/mo                        |
| 1,000  | 100        | 500KB         | ~50 GB       | ~5 GB/mo                          |
| 10,000 | 100        | 500KB         | ~500 GB      | ~50 GB/mo                         |
| 1,000  | 100        | 5MB           | ~500 GB      | ~50 GB/mo                         |

### 4.2 IPNS Name Growth

Each user has:

- 1 vault blob IPNS name
- N folder IPNS names (1 per folder including root)
- M file IPNS names (1 per file)

**Formula:**

```text
ipns_names = users * (1 + avg_folders_per_user + avg_files_per_user)
```

| Users  | Folders/User | Files/User | Total IPNS Names | TEE Republish Batch Size |
| ------ | ------------ | ---------- | ---------------- | ------------------------ |
| 100    | 10           | 100        | ~11,100          | ~11,100 every 6h         |
| 1,000  | 10           | 100        | ~111,000         | ~111,000 every 6h        |
| 10,000 | 10           | 100        | ~1,110,000       | ~1,110,000 every 6h      |

TEE republish batch duration scales linearly with IPNS name count. At current Someguy publish throughput (~15 ops/s), 111,000 names would take ~2 hours to republish -- within the 6-hour window. At 1.1M names, multiple TEE workers or batching optimizations would be needed.

### 4.3 Database Growth

| Table         | Growth Driver             | Rows at 1,000 Users | Rows at 10,000 Users |
| ------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------- | -------------------- |
| users         | 1 per user                | 1,000               | 10,000               |
| vaults        | 1 per user                | 1,000               | 10,000               |
| folder_ipns   | users x (folders + files) | ~111,000            | ~1,110,000           |
| device_tokens | users x avg_devices       | ~2,000              | ~20,000              |

The `folder_ipns` table is the largest growth driver. With proper indexing (already in place on `user_id`, with a unique constraint on `(user_id, ipns_name)`), queries remain efficient at millions of rows.

### 4.4 Cost Estimates (Single Server Deployment)

These are rough estimates for a self-hosted tech demo deployment, not production SLAs.

| Component     | 100 Users      | 1,000 Users     | 10,000 Users     |
| ------------- | -------------- | --------------- | ---------------- |
| VPS (CPU/RAM) | $10-20/mo      | $40-80/mo       | $150-300/mo      |
| Storage (SSD) | $5/mo (50GB)   | $25/mo (250GB)  | $100/mo (1TB)    |
| Bandwidth     | $5/mo          | $20/mo          | $100/mo          |
| Domain/SSL    | $15/yr         | $15/yr          | $15/yr           |
| **Total**     | **~$20-30/mo** | **~$85-125/mo** | **~$350-500/mo** |

**Notes:**

- VPS pricing based on Hostinger/Hetzner tier estimates
- Storage assumes SSD volumes at ~$0.10/GB/mo
- Bandwidth depends heavily on download patterns and provider egress pricing
- Does not include TEE infrastructure costs (Phala Cloud pricing varies)

---

## 5. Load Test Thresholds

Automated pass/fail thresholds are defined in `tests/load/src/harness/thresholds.ts` and integrated into all 8 load test scenarios. Thresholds are 2-3x observed baselines to avoid CI flakiness while still catching significant regressions.

| Scenario           | Operation    | p95 Threshold | Error Rate Max | Rationale                                 |
| ------------------ | ------------ | ------------- | -------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| upload-throughput  | uploadFile   | 10,000ms      | 5%             | 19.2 p95 was 2,841ms at 5 clients (~3.5x) |
| mixed-workload     | uploadFile   | 10,000ms      | 10%            | Mixed has higher error rate historically  |
| mixed-workload     | createFolder | 5,000ms       | 10%            | 19.2 p95 was 936ms at 5 clients (~5x)     |
| ipns-publish-storm | createFolder | 10,000ms      | 10%            | IPNS contention scenario, high variance   |
| sustained-load     | uploadFile   | 10,000ms      | 5%             | Same as upload-throughput                 |
| sustained-load     | createFolder | 5,000ms       | 5%             | Folder ops should stay fast               |
| spike-test (burst) | uploadFile   | 15,000ms      | 15%            | Spike: intentional overload               |
| spike-test (burst) | createFolder | 15,000ms      | 15%            | Spike: intentional overload               |

**How thresholds work:**

1. Each scenario runs its workload and collects `OperationMetrics` via `aggregateAndReport()`
2. `checkThresholds()` compares observed p95 latency and error rate against the threshold table
3. If any threshold is breached, the test fails with a descriptive violation message listing the operation, observed value, and threshold
4. The CI workflow (`load-test.yml`) runs via `workflow_dispatch` (manual trigger), not on every push

**Updating thresholds:** When baselines shift significantly (new infrastructure, new optimizations), update the threshold values in each scenario file. Keep thresholds at 2-3x observed values to maintain a buffer against normal variance.

---

## 7. Retention Consequence of BYO Advisory Rows

### 7.1 Background

CipherBox supports two storage modes for each file CID in `pinned_cids`:

- **Hosted rows**: CIDs pinned via the CipherBox relay (`isByoUser = false`). The CipherBox
  Kubo node physically holds the content.
- **BYO advisory rows**: CIDs registered by BYO-IPFS users (`isByoUser = true`). These rows
  track what the user claims is pinned on their own infrastructure; the CipherBox Kubo node
  does NOT hold these CIDs.

### 7.2 The Retention Consequence

The `guardedUnpin` refcount query counts ALL `pinned_cids` rows for a given CID regardless of
origin — both hosted and BYO advisory rows contribute to the refcount (D-07 design, WR-07
disposition: accepted).

**Consequence:** If a BYO advisory row exists for a CID that is also held by the CipherBox Kubo
node (hosted), deleting the hosted row will NOT trigger a physical unpin of the CID from Kubo
until the BYO advisory row is also removed. The CID is retained in Kubo for as long as any BYO
advisory row references it.

**When this occurs:**

1. User A uploads a file via the CipherBox relay (hosted `pinned_cids` row created).
2. User B (BYO-IPFS mode) registers the same CID (advisory `pinned_cids` row created).
3. User A deletes their file — their hosted row is removed and their quota is decremented
   immediately (D-03), but the CID remains pinned in Kubo because User B's advisory row
   keeps the refcount above zero.
4. Kubo storage is freed only when User B also removes their advisory row.

**Impact on capacity planning:** In environments with significant BYO-IPFS usage, Kubo storage
consumption may exceed what is attributable to hosted users alone. Monitor
`cipherbox_pending_unpin_queue_depth` and `cipherbox_drift_orphaned_pins_total` for divergence
between DB-accounted and Kubo-actual pin counts.

**Operator action:** No action is required — this is intentional design. If an operator needs
to reclaim Kubo storage held by a BYO-referenced CID, they must first remove the BYO advisory
row (e.g., by having the BYO user delete their reference), which will allow the next
`drain-pending-unpins` BullMQ run to physically unpin it.

---

### Baseline Documents

- `.planning/baselines/18-performance-baselines.md` -- Server-side Prometheus baselines (Phase 18)
- `.planning/baselines/19-someguy-ipns-baselines.md` -- IPNS resolution baselines with Someguy sidecar (Phase 19)
- `.planning/baselines/19.2-pre-optimization-baselines.md` -- Upload baselines before concurrent pins + pebbleds

### Architecture

## CipherBox API per-upload delegated-routing (someguy) investigation

### (a) Exact code locations of delegated-routing consumption

The API has exactly ONE consumer of the delegated-routing (someguy) endpoint: `DelegatedRoutingClient`. There are no `findProviders` / `GetProviders` / `provide` / `announce` calls anywhere in `apps/api`, `packages/sdk-core`, or `packages/sdk`.

- `apps/api/src/ipns/delegated-routing.client.ts:27-32` — reads config keys `DELEGATED_ROUTING_URL` (default `https://delegated-ipfs.dev`) and `DELEGATED_ROUTING_FALLBACK_URL` (default empty).
- `delegated-routing.client.ts:48-67` — `publish()` → `PUT /routing/v1/ipns/{name}` (someguy PUT). Primary then optional fallback.
- `delegated-routing.client.ts:75-93` — `resolve()` → `GET /routing/v1/ipns/{name}` (someguy GET). Primary then optional fallback.
- `delegated-routing.client.ts:18-21` — knobs: `maxRetries = 3`, `baseDelayMs = 500`, `maxRetryDelayMs = 30_000`, `requestTimeoutMs = 5_000` (per-request `AbortController` timeout at line 304-317).
- Consumed by `IpnsService`: `apps/api/src/ipns/ipns.service.ts:111-130` (publish, fire-and-forget detached promise) and `ipns.service.ts:470` (resolve, synchronous on `GET /ipns/resolve`).
- Also used by the TEE republish path: `apps/api/src/republish/republish.service.ts` (the 6-hour background re-sign loop — not on the upload path).
- The Kubo pin path (`apps/api/src/ipfs/providers/local.provider.ts` `pinFile`/`unpinFile`/`getFile`, and `apps/api/src/ipfs/ipfs.controller.ts` `/ipfs/upload`) does NOT touch someguy at all — it only calls Kubo `/api/v0/add`, `/pin/rm`, `/cat`.
- Infra: someguy container in `docker/docker-compose.yml:70-98` and `docker/docker-compose.staging.yml:111-137` (limited to `cpus: '1.0'`, `SOMEGUY_DHT: accelerated`). Staging `DELEGATED_ROUTING_URL` is set via the gitignored `.env.staging` (`docker-compose.staging.yml:13` `env_file: .env.staging`) — it points the API at the local someguy container (port 8190).

### (b) Per-upload someguy call list (single file, warm cache, no conflict)

The someguy load is driven entirely by SDK IPNS publishes/resolves relayed through the API. Per `SdkClient.uploadFile` (`packages/sdk/src/client.ts:1005`):

| # | Operation | API endpoint | someguy op | Count | Critical path? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Per-file IPNS record publish | `POST /ipns/publish-batch` (1 entry) | PUT | 1 | Awaited (non-fatal on fail; `client.ts:1067,1090`) |
| 2 | Parent folder IPNS record publish | `POST /ipns/publish` | PUT | 1 | Awaited (fatal on fail; `client.ts:1068,1080`) |
| — | Parent folder resolve | `GET /ipns/resolve` | GET | 0 (warm) | — served from in-memory `folderTree` |
| — | 3× IPFS pin (file ciphertext, file metadata, folder metadata) | `POST /ipfs/upload` | none | 3 | Kubo only, NOT someguy |

Net: 2 someguy PUTs per file upload, 0 GETs (warm). Both PUTs run concurrently in a `Promise.allSettled` (`client.ts:1066`) and are awaited (on the upload critical path).

Important asymmetry: on the API side, each `/ipns/publish` and each `/ipns/publish-batch` entry fires the someguy PUT as a detached/fire-and-forget promise (`ipns.service.ts:105-130`) — the API responds as soon as the DB row is written. So the API HTTP response does NOT block on someguy, but the PUTs are still issued (1 per record) and load someguy out-of-band. The DB is the authoritative source; someguy publish is best-effort DHT propagation.

Cold-cache / conflict variants:
- Cold cache (first touch of a folder): +1 `GET /ipns/resolve` → +1 someguy GET (`client.ts:570,502` → `sdk-core/src/folder/load.ts`).
- 409 CAS conflict on the folder publish: `publishWithCas` re-resolves (`cas.ts:102`) and re-publishes per retry, up to `maxAttempts: 4` → up to +3 GET and +3 PUT.

Per-file IPNS records DO exist: every file gets its own Ed25519 IPNS keypair generated at upload (`sdk-core/src/file/index.ts:114`) and its record is published at sequence 1 on every upload. This is the source of call #1 — it is unconditional per upload.

### (c) Ranked reduction / caching opportunities

1. **Eliminate the per-file IPNS publish from the upload critical path (highest impact).** Every upload publishes a brand-new per-file IPNS record at seq 1 (`file/index.ts`, batch-published at `client.ts:1067`). For a fresh file this someguy PUT carries little value: the file is reachable via the folder's `FilePointer` (which already holds the file CID), and the per-file IPNS name only matters for later in-place file version updates. Options: (i) make the file-record publish lazy — only publish the per-file IPNS record the first time the file is actually mutated/versioned, not at initial upload; or (ii) keep it but drop it from the awaited set (it's already non-fatal) so it never gates upload throughput. Impact: removes ~50% of per-upload someguy PUTs (2→1). Risk: low-medium — must confirm no reader resolves a file's own IPNS name immediately after upload (readers use the folder's FilePointer CID, so likely safe); a lazy scheme needs the per-file keypair persisted in the FilePointer regardless (it already is, `ipnsPrivateKeyEncrypted`).

2. **Batch the folder publish with the file publish into a single `publish-batch` call.** Today uploads issue one `publish-batch` (file) + one `publish` (folder) as two separate API calls (`client.ts:1067-1068`), i.e. two someguy PUTs regardless. Combining into one `publish-batch` does not reduce the PUT count (someguy still does 1 PUT per entry) but halves API round-trips and lets the API's existing batch concurrency limiter (`ipns.service.ts:158`, CONCURRENCY=10) govern someguy fan-out centrally. Impact: low on someguy CPU, moderate on API overhead. Risk: low.

3. **Add server-side de-dup / coalescing of identical someguy PUTs.** Idempotent republishes (same embedded sequence, e.g. TEE re-sign, or a client retry) still issue a someguy PUT (`ipns.service.ts:288-291` updates DB but always calls `delegatedRouting.publish`). A short-TTL "last published (ipnsName, sequence)" guard in `DelegatedRoutingClient`/`IpnsService` could skip a PUT when the exact record was just pushed. Impact: medium under load with retries/republish overlap. Risk: low — DB remains source of truth.

4. **There is no resolve-side cache in the API.** `GET /ipns/resolve` always hits someguy first, then merges with DB (`ipns.service.ts:469-491`). On the upload path this is 0 calls (warm SDK `folderTree`), so it does not affect upload throughput — but under read-heavy load (30 resolves/min/user, `ipns.controller.ts:156`) it is a someguy GET amplifier. A short-TTL in-process or Redis cache keyed by `ipnsName` (the DB row is already effectively a cache and is often ahead of someguy) would cut resolve GETs substantially. Impact: high for read load, neutral for the upload benchmark in question. Risk: medium (staleness; mitigated by short TTL + existing DB-vs-network higher-sequence-wins logic).

5. **Tune someguy itself / split publish vs resolve load.** someguy at `cpus: 1.0` with `SOMEGUY_DHT: accelerated` runs an accelerated DHT client, which is CPU-heavy. The PUT path (provide/publish to DHT) is the expensive one. Raising the someguy CPU limit, or pointing publishes at the public `delegated-ipfs.dev` (as `DELEGATED_ROUTING_FALLBACK_URL` already can) while keeping local someguy only for what truly needs it, would relieve the bottleneck. Impact: high. Risk: low-medium (cost / external dependency / rate limits on public endpoint).

### (d) Notes on the premise

The premise holds and is sharpened by the code:

- Confirmed: per-upload someguy load originates in the API/SDK (the IPNS `publish` PUTs), not Kubo. Kubo's pin path never calls delegated routing.
- Refinement: there are exactly 2 someguy PUTs per warm-cache upload (file record + folder record), and 0 GETs — the resolve path does not contribute to the upload benchmark because the SDK's in-memory `folderTree` cache (`client.ts:65`, adopted post-publish at `client.ts:1121-1124`) serves the folder without a network resolve. So the someguy CPU spike during upload-throughput load is PUT-dominated, not resolve-dominated.
- Subtlety re "critical path": on the API side the someguy PUT is fire-and-forget (`ipns.service.ts:111`) — the API HTTP response returns after the DB write, not after someguy. So throttling someguy throttled upload throughput not via the synchronous API response, but because (a) the SDK awaits both publish API calls and (b) someguy, when starved, back-pressures the whole pipeline (slow/queued PUTs, connection contention, accelerated-DHT CPU saturation). The cheapest win is therefore reducing the number of PUTs issued per upload (opportunities 1 and 3), since the API does not actually need someguy to be fast to return — it needs someguy to not be overwhelmed by the volume of best-effort PUTs.

Key files: `apps/api/src/ipns/delegated-routing.client.ts`, `apps/api/src/ipns/ipns.service.ts`, `apps/api/src/ipns/ipns.controller.ts`, `apps/api/src/ipfs/providers/local.provider.ts`, `packages/sdk/src/client.ts` (uploadFile ~1005), `packages/sdk-core/src/cas.ts`, `packages/sdk-core/src/file/index.ts`, `packages/sdk-core/src/ipns/index.ts`, `docker/docker-compose.staging.yml`.</result>

**Latest stable is Kubo v0.42.0** (2026-06-08); we're on **v0.40.0**, so this spans 0.41 → 0.42. Two things make this more than a one-line bump:

1. **It's wide** — `ipfs/kubo:v0.40.0` appears in 2 compose files, **6 CI workflows** (incl. `--filter ancestor=ipfs/kubo:v0.40.0` in `web-e2e.yml`/`deploy-landing.yml`, which must match the running image exactly), and 2 docs. All must move in lockstep. (I'll leave `.planning/` history alone.)
2. **It carries migration risk** — 0.40 already FATAL'd us on a deprecated config key. 0.41/0.42 could do the same or bump the fs-repo version (one-way migration).

So I'm vetting the 0.41/0.42 changelogs before bumping (sub-agent launched), and since I have staging access I'll validate the v0.42.0 image boots cleanly with our `Provide.Strategy: roots` config before the PR merges. Launching the vet + reading the staging compose to start the edits:

input.description: Vet Kubo 0.41/0.42 changelogs
input.prompt:
Research the upgrade risk of bumping Kubo (go-ipfs) from v0.40.0 to v0.42.0 for a production-ish deployment. We are jumping across v0.41.0 and v0.42.0.

Authoritative sources to fetch (use WebFetch/WebSearch):
- https://github.com/ipfs/kubo/releases/tag/v0.41.0
- https://github.com/ipfs/kubo/releases/tag/v0.42.0
- The changelog files: https://github.com/ipfs/kubo/blob/master/docs/changelogs/v0.41.md and https://github.com/ipfs/kubo/blob/master/docs/changelogs/v0.42.md (try the raw URLs if the blob view is hard to parse: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ipfs/kubo/master/docs/changelogs/v0.41.md and .../v0.42.md)

Our current setup that MUST keep working:
- Docker image ipfs/kubo, env IPFS_PROFILE=server,pebbleds (pebbleds LSM-tree datastore).
- Config: Provide.Strategy=roots (Kubo 0.40 renamed Reprovider.Strategy -> Provide.Strategy; we already migrated and REMOVED the deprecated Reprovider.* keys from the repo config).
- We rely on the Provide/Reprovide system and DHT announcement of pin roots.
- A persistent named volume holds the fs-repo (we do NOT want a surprise one-way repo migration to silently break a rollback).

Report (concise markdown, do NOT write files) covering, for v0.41.0 and v0.42.0 SPECIFICALLY:
1. BREAKING CHANGES — especially any config key that is deprecated/removed/renamed and causes a FATAL on boot if present (the way Reprovider did in 0.40). List each with the exact key and required action.
2. fs-repo version / migration — does 0.41 or 0.42 bump the repo version requiring an automatic (one-way) migration on first boot? Is it automatic in the docker image? Any downgrade caveats.
3. Changes to the Provide / Reprovide / DHT-announcement system — anything that affects Provide.Strategy=roots semantics, new Provide.* keys, new defaults, the "sweeping DHT provider" / accelerated provide work, etc.
4. pebbleds / Datastore changes that affect server,pebbleds profile.
5. Go version, default config, gateway/RPC changes that could affect a node behind a reverse proxy with API/gateway on loopback.
6. Any NEW recommended config for our use case (e.g. if 0.41/0.42 introduced a better provide strategy or a knob to reduce provider CPU).

End with a clear VERDICT: is bumping 0.40.0 -> 0.42.0 safe for our config as-is, what (if any) config/init changes are required first, and whether a one-way repo migration will occur. Cite the source for each breaking-change claim. Read-only; do not modify files or run anything.

- `apps/api/src/ipns/delegated-routing.client.ts:27-32` — reads config keys `DELEGATED_ROUTING_URL` (default `https://delegated-ipfs.dev`) and `DELEGATED_ROUTING_FALLBACK_URL` (default empty).
- `delegated-routing.client.ts:48-67` — `publish()` → `PUT /routing/v1/ipns/{name}` (someguy PUT). Primary then optional fallback.
- `delegated-routing.client.ts:75-93` — `resolve()` → `GET /routing/v1/ipns/{name}` (someguy GET). Primary then optional fallback.
- `delegated-routing.client.ts:18-21` — knobs: `maxRetries = 3`, `baseDelayMs = 500`, `maxRetryDelayMs = 30_000`, `requestTimeoutMs = 5_000` (per-request `AbortController` timeout at line 304-317).
- Consumed by `IpnsService`: `apps/api/src/ipns/ipns.service.ts:111-130` (publish, fire-and-forget detached promise) and `ipns.service.ts:470` (resolve, synchronous on `GET /ipns/resolve`).
- Also used by the TEE republish path: `apps/api/src/republish/republish.service.ts` (the 6-hour background re-sign loop — not on the upload path).
- The Kubo pin path (`apps/api/src/ipfs/providers/local.provider.ts` `pinFile`/`unpinFile`/`getFile`, and `apps/api/src/ipfs/ipfs.controller.ts` `/ipfs/upload`) does NOT touch someguy at all — it only calls Kubo `/api/v0/add`, `/pin/rm`, `/cat`.
- Infra: someguy container in `docker/docker-compose.yml:70-98` and `docker/docker-compose.staging.yml:111-137` (limited to `cpus: '1.0'`, `SOMEGUY_DHT: accelerated`). Staging `DELEGATED_ROUTING_URL` is set via the gitignored `.env.staging` (`docker-compose.staging.yml:13` `env_file: .env.staging`) — it points the API at the local someguy container (port 8190).

### (b) Per-upload someguy call list (single file, warm cache, no conflict)

The someguy load is driven entirely by SDK IPNS publishes/resolves relayed through the API. Per `SdkClient.uploadFile` (`packages/sdk/src/client.ts:1005`):

| # | Operation | API endpoint | someguy op | Count | Critical path? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Per-file IPNS record publish | `POST /ipns/publish-batch` (1 entry) | PUT | 1 | Awaited (non-fatal on fail; `client.ts:1067,1090`) |
| 2 | Parent folder IPNS record publish | `POST /ipns/publish` | PUT | 1 | Awaited (fatal on fail; `client.ts:1068,1080`) |
| — | Parent folder resolve | `GET /ipns/resolve` | GET | 0 (warm) | — served from in-memory `folderTree` |
| — | 3× IPFS pin (file ciphertext, file metadata, folder metadata) | `POST /ipfs/upload` | none | 3 | Kubo only, NOT someguy |

Net: 2 someguy PUTs per file upload, 0 GETs (warm). Both PUTs run concurrently in a `Promise.allSettled` (`client.ts:1066`) and are awaited (on the upload critical path).

Important asymmetry: on the API side, each `/ipns/publish` and each `/ipns/publish-batch` entry fires the someguy PUT as a detached/fire-and-forget promise (`ipns.service.ts:105-130`) — the API responds as soon as the DB row is written. So the API HTTP response does NOT block on someguy, but the PUTs are still issued (1 per record) and load someguy out-of-band. The DB is the authoritative source; someguy publish is best-effort DHT propagation.

Cold-cache / conflict variants:
- Cold cache (first touch of a folder): +1 `GET /ipns/resolve` → +1 someguy GET (`client.ts:570,502` → `sdk-core/src/folder/load.ts`).
- 409 CAS conflict on the folder publish: `publishWithCas` re-resolves (`cas.ts:102`) and re-publishes per retry, up to `maxAttempts: 4` → up to +3 GET and +3 PUT.

Per-file IPNS records DO exist: every file gets its own Ed25519 IPNS keypair generated at upload (`sdk-core/src/file/index.ts:114`) and its record is published at sequence 1 on every upload. This is the source of call #1 — it is unconditional per upload.

### (c) Ranked reduction / caching opportunities

1. **Eliminate the per-file IPNS publish from the upload critical path (highest impact).** Every upload publishes a brand-new per-file IPNS record at seq 1 (`file/index.ts`, batch-published at `client.ts:1067`). For a fresh file this someguy PUT carries little value: the file is reachable via the folder's `FilePointer` (which already holds the file CID), and the per-file IPNS name only matters for later in-place file version updates. Options: (i) make the file-record publish lazy — only publish the per-file IPNS record the first time the file is actually mutated/versioned, not at initial upload; or (ii) keep it but drop it from the awaited set (it's already non-fatal) so it never gates upload throughput. Impact: removes ~50% of per-upload someguy PUTs (2→1). Risk: low-medium — must confirm no reader resolves a file's own IPNS name immediately after upload (readers use the folder's FilePointer CID, so likely safe); a lazy scheme needs the per-file keypair persisted in the FilePointer regardless (it already is, `ipnsPrivateKeyEncrypted`).

2. **Batch the folder publish with the file publish into a single `publish-batch` call.** Today uploads issue one `publish-batch` (file) + one `publish` (folder) as two separate API calls (`client.ts:1067-1068`), i.e. two someguy PUTs regardless. Combining into one `publish-batch` does not reduce the PUT count (someguy still does 1 PUT per entry) but halves API round-trips and lets the API's existing batch concurrency limiter (`ipns.service.ts:158`, CONCURRENCY=10) govern someguy fan-out centrally. Impact: low on someguy CPU, moderate on API overhead. Risk: low.

3. **Add server-side de-dup / coalescing of identical someguy PUTs.** Idempotent republishes (same embedded sequence, e.g. TEE re-sign, or a client retry) still issue a someguy PUT (`ipns.service.ts:288-291` updates DB but always calls `delegatedRouting.publish`). A short-TTL "last published (ipnsName, sequence)" guard in `DelegatedRoutingClient`/`IpnsService` could skip a PUT when the exact record was just pushed. Impact: medium under load with retries/republish overlap. Risk: low — DB remains source of truth.

4. **There is no resolve-side cache in the API.** `GET /ipns/resolve` always hits someguy first, then merges with DB (`ipns.service.ts:469-491`). On the upload path this is 0 calls (warm SDK `folderTree`), so it does not affect upload throughput — but under read-heavy load (30 resolves/min/user, `ipns.controller.ts:156`) it is a someguy GET amplifier. A short-TTL in-process or Redis cache keyed by `ipnsName` (the DB row is already effectively a cache and is often ahead of someguy) would cut resolve GETs substantially. Impact: high for read load, neutral for the upload benchmark in question. Risk: medium (staleness; mitigated by short TTL + existing DB-vs-network higher-sequence-wins logic).

5. **Tune someguy itself / split publish vs resolve load.** someguy at `cpus: 1.0` with `SOMEGUY_DHT: accelerated` runs an accelerated DHT client, which is CPU-heavy. The PUT path (provide/publish to DHT) is the expensive one. Raising the someguy CPU limit, or pointing publishes at the public `delegated-ipfs.dev` (as `DELEGATED_ROUTING_FALLBACK_URL` already can) while keeping local someguy only for what truly needs it, would relieve the bottleneck. Impact: high. Risk: low-medium (cost / external dependency / rate limits on public endpoint).

### (d) Notes on the premise

The premise holds and is sharpened by the code:

- Confirmed: per-upload someguy load originates in the API/SDK (the IPNS `publish` PUTs), not Kubo. Kubo's pin path never calls delegated routing.
- Refinement: there are exactly 2 someguy PUTs per warm-cache upload (file record + folder record), and 0 GETs — the resolve path does not contribute to the upload benchmark because the SDK's in-memory `folderTree` cache (`client.ts:65`, adopted post-publish at `client.ts:1121-1124`) serves the folder without a network resolve. So the someguy CPU spike during upload-throughput load is PUT-dominated, not resolve-dominated.
- Subtlety re "critical path": on the API side the someguy PUT is fire-and-forget (`ipns.service.ts:111`) — the API HTTP response returns after the DB write, not after someguy. So throttling someguy throttled upload throughput not via the synchronous API response, but because (a) the SDK awaits both publish API calls and (b) someguy, when starved, back-pressures the whole pipeline (slow/queued PUTs, connection contention, accelerated-DHT CPU saturation). The cheapest win is therefore reducing the number of PUTs issued per upload (opportunities 1 and 3), since the API does not actually need someguy to be fast to return — it needs someguy to not be overwhelmed by the volume of best-effort PUTs.

#!/bin/sh
# CipherBox Kubo init: announce only pin roots to the DHT, not every block.
#
# Reduces background provide/reprovide CPU on the shared Kubo node. With the
# default "all" strategy the staging node scheduled ~76k CIDs for DHT
# announcement, consuming a large share of Kubo's CPU at idle; "roots" cuts that
# to the pin-root count (~18k) with no loss of retrievability (every pinned root
# is still announced; only unpinned intermediate blocks are dropped).
#
# Kubo 0.40 renamed Reprovider.Strategy -> Provide.Strategy. This file is sourced
# by the Kubo entrypoint on every boot (before the daemon starts), so the setting
# is idempotent and survives container recreation and fresh repos.
ipfs config Provide.Strategy roots || echo "ipfs-init: failed to set Provide.Strategy roots (continuing)"

<result>Confirmed: both v0.40.0 and v0.42.0 use `RepoVersion = 18`. No repo migration occurs across the jump. I now have everything verified against authoritative sources.

# Kubo v0.40.0 → v0.42.0 Upgrade Risk Report

Scope: jumping across v0.41.0 and v0.42.0, for a Docker `ipfs/kubo` node with `IPFS_PROFILE=server,pebbleds`, `Provide.Strategy=roots`, deprecated `Reprovider.*` keys already removed, on a persistent fs-repo volume.

## 1. Breaking changes / fatal-on-boot config keys

| Version | Breaking item | Applies to us? | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| v0.41.0 | None labeled "Breaking." Only behavioral note: `ipfs files chcid /` (MFS root) no longer accepted. | No | None |
| v0.42.0 | `[!IMPORTANT]` — daemon **refuses to start when `Provide.DHT.Interval=0` is set without an explicit `Provide.Enabled`**. | **No** — only triggers if you have `Provide.DHT.Interval=0`. Our config uses `Provide.Strategy=roots` and does not set `Interval=0`. | None required. (If you ever set `Interval=0`, you must also set `Provide.Enabled=false` or `=true`.) |

There is **no key that fatals on boot for our config** in either release — unlike the `Reprovider.*` removal in 0.40. `Provide.Strategy=roots` is unchanged and still valid in both releases. No config keys are removed or renamed in 0.41 or 0.42. (Sources: v0.42 changelog `[!IMPORTANT]` block; v0.41 changelog has no Breaking section — confirmed "NOT PRESENT".)

## 2. fs-repo version / migration

**No repo migration occurs.** Verified directly from source: `version.go` defines `const RepoVersion = 18` in **both v0.40.0 and v0.42.0** (and 0.41 sits between, same value). Since the on-disk repo version is unchanged, first boot on 0.42.0 performs **no one-way fs-repo migration** — rollback to 0.40.0 is safe at the repo-format level.

Caveats:
- v0.41 does a transparent, automatic one-time cleanup: the provider keystore relocates to `$IPFS_PATH/provider-keystore/` and stale keystore data is purged from the shared datastore on first start. This is not a repo-version migration and is not gated by repo version, but it does mutate the datastore — take a volume snapshot before upgrading if you want a clean rollback.
- The only "migration" text in the 0.42 changelog refers to the legacy one-time migration for repos older than **v0.27** (gateway-download robustness). Irrelevant to a repo already at v18.

(Sources: `version.go` at tags v0.40.0 and v0.42.0 = `RepoVersion = 18`; v0.41 changelog keystore-relocation note; v0.42 changelog migration note scoped to pre-v0.27.)

## 3. Provide / Reprovide / DHT-announcement changes

`Provide.Strategy=roots` semantics are preserved. Notable additions/changes:

- **v0.42 — pinner lock fix (positive for us):** the pinner no longer holds a read lock for the whole reprovide cycle for `roots` (and `pinned`, `pinned+mfs`, `+unique`/`+entities`). The index is snapshotted under the lock then released, eliminating multi-hour blocking of `ipfs pin ls` / `ipfs add` during reprovide. Default `all` was unaffected; `roots` benefits directly.
- **v0.42 — new `ipfs provide once <cid>`** for immediate announcement (streams from stdin); `ipfs routing provide` is now deprecated. Additive.
- **v0.42 — new `Provide.DHT.SendProviderRecordTimeout`** caps per-peer provider-record sends so unresponsive peers can't stall reprovide cycles. Additive, has a default.
- **v0.42 — `Provide.DHT.Interval=0` semantic change:** now disables only the periodic reprovide schedule (new CIDs still announce via fast-provide-root / `provide once`); full disable is `Provide.Enabled=false`. Only relevant if you set `Interval=0` (see §1).
- **v0.41 — new strategy modifiers** `+unique` (bloom-dedup across recursive pins) and `+entities` (announce only entity roots, skip internal chunks), plus `Provide.BloomFPRate`. Additive; defaults unchanged for `roots`.

(Source: v0.42 changelog pinner-lock + `provide once` + `SendProviderRecordTimeout` + `Interval=0` notes; v0.41 changelog strategy modifiers + `BloomFPRate`.)

## 4. pebbleds / Datastore changes (server,pebbleds)

- No breaking schema changes for pebble; profile string `pebbleds` is unchanged and valid.
- **v0.42:** pinner now cancels and waits for in-flight pin work before the datastore closes — removes `"pebble: closed"` panic traces from shutdown logs. Pure robustness improvement.
- **v0.41:** provider keystore moved out of the shared datastore into `$IPFS_PATH/provider-keystore/`; after each reprovide cycle the old keystore datastore is removed from disk, reclaiming space immediately (fixes unbounded `datastore/` growth with DHT sweep). Affects all backends including pebble; transparent.

(Source: v0.42 changelog pebble-shutdown note; v0.41 changelog keystore relocation.)

## 5. Go version, default config, gateway/RPC behind reverse proxy

- **Go:** v0.41 returns to Go 1.26.2 (after a 0.40.1 downgrade); v0.42 → Go 1.26.4. Lower memory / reduced GC pauses (Green Tea GC). No action.
- **Reverse-proxy / loopback gotcha (applies to both 0.41 and 0.42):** the `server` profile's `Swarm.AddrFilters` includes `/ip4/127.0.0.0/ipcidr/8`, which blocks loopback **swarm** listeners. v0.42 now logs one ERROR per blocked listener.

**Mean pin latency:** 1.37s (down from 1.73s pre-optimization, -20.8%)

### 1.5 Re-baseline (2026-06): provider CPU and someguy contention

A 2026-06 staging re-baseline (upload-throughput @ 50 clients) measured ~10 ops/s versus the 15.10 ops/s recorded in Phase 19.2 (§1.2). Object count was ruled out as the cause: a garbage-collection from 294,811 to 20,038 datastore objects did not change throughput.

CPU-limit sweep (all runs share the same datastore state, `Provide.Strategy=roots`, on the 2 vCPU staging host):

| ipfs cpus | someguy cpus | uploadFile p50 | uploadFile p95 | Throughput  |
| --------- | ------------ | -------------- | -------------- | ----------- |
| 1.0       | 1.0          | 5,779ms        | 8,001ms        | 8.71 ops/s  |
| 1.5       | 1.0          | 4,894ms        | 6,506ms        | 10.28 ops/s |
| 2.0       | 1.0          | 5,105ms        | 7,385ms        | 9.80 ops/s  |
| 2.0       | 0.4          | 5,855ms        | 7,501ms        | 8.66 ops/s  |

Findings:

- **Two cores are the wall.** During load, ipfs and someguy together saturate the host's two cores (combined CPU 160-176% of 200%). Raising ipfs past 1.5 gives nothing (2.0 ties 1.5) because the physical cores, shared with someguy, are the ceiling. 1.5 is the measured knee (+18% over 1.0).
- **someguy is a per-upload participant, not a parasite.** Each upload publishes two IPNS records through the API's delegated-routing client (someguy): one per-file record and one parent-folder record. Throttling someguy to 0.4 made throughput _worse_ (8.66 ops/s) by bottlenecking the publish path - it is on the critical path and must not be starved.
- **Object count is not the throughput driver** (GC test above). It affects background provide/DHT CPU, which `Provide.Strategy=roots` already bounds to the pin-root count (~18k roots vs ~76k blocks under the default `all`).
- **Hardware note:** the host is a 2 vCPU / 8 GB / 100 GB NVMe plan. §1.1 records a 4 vCPU baseline host; that figure is unverified and inconsistent with the current plan, so cross-baseline comparisons against the 15.10 ops/s figure may not be same-hardware.

Applied remediation (PR): Kubo upgraded v0.40.0 -> v0.42.0, ipfs limits raised to `cpus: 1.5` / `memory: 3G`, `Provide.Strategy=roots` made reproducible via a `/container-init.d` script. Recommended next: upgrade the host to >= 4 vCPU (or move someguy to its own cores) and defer the per-file IPNS publish off the upload critical path (§3.2).
